cemetery_profile.name: South-View Cemetery
distinction: Oldest African American cemetery in Atlanta

Founded by formerly enslaved African American businessmen

cemetery_profile.founding_story: South-View Cemetery was founded in response to the indignities African Americans faced at Atlanta's segregated burial grounds. Oakland Cemetery (est. 1850) maintained a 'Slave Square,' and in 1877 the Atlanta City Council ordered the exhumation and mass reinterment of its 860+ occupants to resell the land to white buyers. Westview Cemetery (est. 1884) confined African Americans to a segregated section called 'Rest Haven,' accessible only through a back gate. Albert Watts watched his father Sterling Watts buried through that back gate in October 1885. Six months later, on April 26, 1886, Watts and five other formerly enslaved men chartered South-View Cemetery Association — a burial ground owned and controlled entirely by African Americans.

historical_context.topic: Racial Segregation in Atlanta Cemeteries — Why South-View Was Founded
historical_context.content: Until the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, Atlanta's cemeteries were segregated by law and tradition. Oakland Cemetery (est. 1850) designated 'Slave Square' in 1852 — a section for both free and enslaved African Americans. By the Civil War's end, 860+ people were buried there. In 1877, the Atlanta City Council voted to exhume Slave Square, rebury the remains in the colored pauper grounds (many anonymously in a mass grave), and resell the lots. The exact location of their reburial remains unknown. Westview Cemetery (est. 1884) maintained 'Rest Haven,' a segregated section for African Americans accessible only through a back gate several hundred yards past the main entrance. These indignities — combined with African American petitions to the city council in early 1878 for either additional burial space or a separate cemetery — directly motivated the founding of South-View in 1886.

historical_context.topic: Founding and Early History of South-View Cemetery
historical_context.content: South-View Cemetery Association was chartered April 26, 1886 — six months after Albert Watts watched his father buried through Westview's back gate. The first organizational meeting was held at Friendship Baptist Church. Early investors included fraternal orders (Grand United Order of Odd Fellows) and church benevolent societies (Daughters of Bethel). South-View claims the distinction of being the oldest African American stockholder corporation in the United States. The cemetery was originally 25 acres; by 1946 it had expanded to approximately 90 acres; it now covers over 100 acres. In 1961, the cemetery dedicated a monument to its founders and early board members, listing charter members and 16 deceased board members including Alonzo F. Herndon, David T. Howard, and Charles S. Cox. Mary L. Bentley, office manager for 48 years, is the sole woman named on the memorial as of 2017.

historical_context.topic: Categories of Notable Residents at South-View
historical_context.content: South-View's historic section reflects the full breadth of African American life in Atlanta. Notable early burials include Alonzo F. Herndon (Atlanta Life Insurance founder, Atlanta's first Black millionaire); Bishop Henry McNeal Turner (AME leader, Reconstruction legislator); George Wilder and Frank Smith (killed in the 1906 Atlanta Race Riot). 20th-century notables include Moses Amos (Georgia's first licensed Black pharmacist); Alice Dugged Cary (first Auburn Avenue Library librarian); 1st Lt. Walter Westmoreland (Tuskegee Airman); John Wesley Dobbs ('Mayor of Sweet Auburn'); Grace Towns Hamilton (first Black woman in Georgia legislature); Julian Bond (scholar, civil rights activist); Hank Aaron (baseball legend); Herman J. Russell (entrepreneur). Atlanta Child Murder victims buried at South-View: Milton Harvey, Yusef Bell, Aaron Wyche, Aaron Jackson, Patrick Rogers, Curtis Walker, William Barrett. 21st-century notables include Jesse Hill Jr. (first Black chair, Georgia Board of Regents); Asa Yancey (first Black faculty at Emory Medical School); Mattiwilda Dobbs (first Black at La Scala opera). Originally buried here but moved: Martin Luther King Jr. (1968, now at MLK Center), Lt. Henry Ossian Flipper (1940, reinterred Thomasville, GA), Dr. Benjamin E. Mays (1984, moved to Morehouse memorial).

historical_context.topic: South-View Cemetery and the Civil Rights Movement
historical_context.content: South-View is inseparable from Atlanta's Civil Rights history. Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King (MLK Jr.'s parents) are interred in a marble crypt at South-View. All deceased pastors of historic Ebenezer Baptist Church (as of 2016) are buried here. Fred C. Bennette (d. 1994) was one of MLK Jr.'s closest aides; his epitaph was written by Andrew Young. Theodore Martin Alexander provided Lloyd's of London liability insurance for cars used in the Montgomery Bus Boycott. Grace Towns Hamilton was the first Black woman elected to any Deep South state legislature (Georgia, 1965). Jesse Hill Jr. was the first Black member and chair of the Georgia Board of Regents. Julian Bond (1940-2015) — scholar, SNCC co-founder, NAACP chair — is buried here. MLK Jr. himself was temporarily buried at South-View in 1968 before being moved to the King Center.

historical_context.topic: Atlanta Child Murder Victims Buried at South-View
historical_context.content: From 1979 to 1981, approximately 29 African American children, teenagers, and young adults were kidnapped and murdered in Atlanta in what became known as the Atlanta Child Murders. Several victims' families chose South-View Cemetery as their sons' final resting place. Victims buried at South-View include: Milton Harvey, Yusef Bell, Aaron Wyche, Aaron Jackson, Patrick Rogers, Curtis Walker, and William Barrett.

historical_context.topic: Funerary Art, Symbolism, and Memorial Traditions at South-View
historical_context.content: South-View's landscape reflects 19th-century garden cemetery aesthetics combined with African American vernacular traditions. Victorian funerary symbols throughout the historic section include obelisks, urns, and angels. Fraternal and benevolent order symbols — Odd Fellows, Masons, Good Samaritans — appear on many markers. Children's gravestones often feature lambs, flowers, and cradle imagery. Vernacular African American traditions include concrete aggregate markers (manufactured locally by Eldren Bailey), seashells, and personal items placed on graves. Cedar and yucca plants are traditional plantings. Adinkra symbols from West African (Akan/Ghana) tradition are referenced in the book's illustrations. Epitaphs range from biblical verse to fraternal mottos to personal tributes — Fred Bennette's gravestone bears the motto 'Commandante' with an epitaph written by Andrew Young.

historical_context.topic: African American Funeral Industry Connected to South-View
historical_context.content: South-View was central to Atlanta's African American funeral industry during segregation. David T. Howard (undertaker) was an original South-View board member and investor. Cox Brothers Funeral Home was founded in 1900 by Emily Griffin Cox with her sons Allen and Charles S. Cox; Charles's widow, Addie G. Turner Cox Barksdale, later managed it. Geneva Moton Haugabrooks opened Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue in 1929. Henry M. Ivey was an undertaker listed on the South-View memorial. Eldren Matthew Bailey (d. 1987) ran a small business manufacturing distinctive concrete grave markers for Atlanta's African American funeral homes — these markers are a vernacular art form documented throughout South-View's historic section. Appendix B of the source book lists early African American undertakers and funeral homes in Atlanta.

historical_context.topic: African American Fraternal and Benevolent Organizations at South-View
historical_context.content: During segregation, African American fraternal and benevolent organizations provided social insurance, community support, and political organizing. Many organizations purchased group burial lots at South-View. Organizations represented include: Grand United Order of Odd Fellows; Prince Hall Masons; Daughters of Bethel; Good Samaritans; and various church benevolent societies affiliated with AME, Baptist, Methodist, and Congregational churches. The Leonard Street Orphans Home has a burial lot in South-View's historic section. Appendix A of the source book lists early African American benevolent organizations in Atlanta.

people.biography: Educator. Adams was the daughter of pioneer Atlantans Wesley and Ellen Redding. She earned her teaching credentials at Atlanta University, and she taught in the Atlanta and Fulton County schools and at the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home. Adams served as the historian for First Congregational Church, and she was a member of the board of directors of the Auburn Avenue Research Library. As one of the oldest residents of Auburn Avenue, she was well known for her in-depth knowledge of Atlanta history.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Clubwoman, Church Worker. Alexander was active in women's club work and served as president of both the Atlanta Federation of Women's Clubs and the Georgia Federation of Women's Clubs. She was second vice president of the National Association of Women's Clubs. Alexander graduated from the Fair Haven Infirmary nursing school at Morris Brown College and also received a degree from Turner Theological Seminary. A member of Allen Temple, she served in various positions in the AME church, including membership on the National AME Judicial Council. Alexander endowed a chair of religious education at Morris Brown College. She married John Alexander Jr.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Alexander was a motherless, barefoot boy of six when his father brought him and his siblings to Atlanta in search of a better life. Considered a self-made man noted for his thrift, at the time of his death, John Alexander was one of the wealthiest African Americans in Atlanta. He operated a meat market on Fraser Street and owned numerous properties in the city. He was an active member and supporter of Allen Temple AME Church where he served as treasurer of the building fund and assisted the congregation with their land acquisitions.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Insurance Company Owner. Alexander founded Alexander & Company, one of the nation's most successful African American insurance agencies. He served as president of the Empire Real Estate Board, organized by African American real estate professionals in Atlanta in 1939. Alexander was a graduate of Morehouse College and a friend of Martin Luther King, Jr. He served as president of the NAACP Atlanta branch. After auto insurance was denied by white American companies, Alexander provided liability insurance underwritten by Lloyd's of London for cars used in the Montgomery bus boycott. President Lyndon Johnson appointed Alexander as advisor to the National Citizens Committee for Human Relations to aid in the implementation of the 1964 Civil Rights Act. He married Dorothy E. Hudson.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She attended the Fashion Academy of New York before opening her own interior design business in 1961. She served on the National Voluntary Service Advisory Council with U.S. First Lady Patricia Nixon, and she was recognized for her social service work by the National Council of Negro Women, the NAACP, and the Atlanta Urban League. Along with Bennie McLendon, she led the protest to desegregate the annual performances of the Metropolitan Opera at Atlanta's Fox Theater.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Pharmacist. Following in the footsteps of his uncle Moses Amos, Georgia's first African American licensed pharmacist, Miles Amos became proprietor of the West Side Drug Store upon his uncle's death in 1928. The next year the store began advertising as Amos' Drugstore. Amos worked his way through Wilberforce College in Ohio with a summer job as a Pullman Porter. He graduated from Cincinnati College of Pharmacy in 1928. In 1953, Amos and two other African Americans, Austin Thomas Walden and Roderick Badger Harris, won a court decision to qualify for election to the City Executive Committee, a nonpartisan political organization responsible for conducting Atlanta's primary elections. Amos won over Harris, and Walden ran unopposed. He married his cousin India DeLaine Amos.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was the daughter of Moses and Emma Amos. She was a graduate of Atlanta public schools and Fisk University in Nashville, Tennessee. She assisted in the operations of Amos' Drugstore until she and her husband both retired in 1969.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: In June 1911, Amos passed the Georgia state pharmacy exam and became the first African American granted a druggist license by the Georgia State Board of Pharmacy. He was married to Emma L. Holmes.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Moses Amos.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Andrews was the first African American registered nurse in Georgia. Though the Grady Memorial Hospital School of Nursing opened in 1898, African Americans were not offered training until 1914 when Andrews organized the Grady Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses. She served as superintendent of the school until 1922. Beginning in 1922, Grady's white American nursing officials began directing the school; in 1965, the two schools were combined. The National Conclave of Grady Graduate Nurses preserves the history of the African American nursing school and Andrew's legacy as its founder. Andrews was superintendent of the Mac Vicar Hospital at Spelman College from 1928 to 1948. She graduated from Mac Vicar's nurse training program in 1906 and that same year was hired as superintendent of Atlanta's Lula Grove Training School for Colored Nurses. Andrews was involved in many health and community service organizations-she was an original board member of the Atlanta Urban League, volunteered with the Community Chest, served as a board member in the colored branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association, and was a life member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA. She was a charter member of the Neighborhood Union and served as its second president from 1937 to 1942. A community center for African Americans in Gainesville, Georgia, was named in her honor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Archer served as fifth president of Morehouse College from 1931 until 1938. He married a classmate, Anna Courbley Johnson (d. 1946 ), whom he met at Wayland Academy in Washington, D. C. The two competed academically for highest honors, and she often insisted that she came in second only because of male preference. Before her marriage to Archer, she taught in the public schools in Princeton, New Jersey. When the couple moved to Atlanta, she served Morehouse in numerous ways-from heating water for injured football players to serving as dormitory matron, library assistant, and dietician. She was studying toward a degree at Morehouse at the time of her husband's death.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Church Worker. A graduate of Clark College and Northwestern University in Chicago, Illinois, Arnold was voted teacher of the year at Turner High School in 1957. A popular public speaker, Arnold died in a car crash while on route to speak at a meeting of the Women's International League of Peace and Freedom in Wisconsin.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Austin was ten years old when slavery ended. His education included only a few years at a small church school, Perry Chapel, in Franklin County, Georgia. With his partner, W. A Stovall, Austin opened the first barbershop owned by African Americans on Auburn Avenue. In their later years, Austin and his wife Adline ( d. 1938) began working as butler and cook for the C. T. Latsons, a white American family. As Mrs. Latson lay dying. she asked Adline to continue taking care of the younger Latson daughter, Leola. When Leola was to be engaged, her suitor asked Adline's approval. Adline agreed, with the condition that the young man treat Leola well, "If you can 't be good to her, why just bring her right back to me." Upon C. T. Latson's death, Adline received a bequest, the same amount given to his children. After Austin's retirement, at Leola's request, Austin began receiving a monthly pension from the Latson family. Austin died at age ninety-five.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Plasterer, Grave Digger, Artist. Bailey started a small business that manufactured grave markers for Atlanta's African American funeral homes.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. She managed Cox Brothers Funeral Home, established in Atlanta in 1900 by her husband Charles S. Cox and his family.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. Bearden was pastor of Big Bethel AME Church in the 1950s and 60s. He was a graduate of Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. An outspoken civil rights leader, he used his weekly radio broadcasts from Big Bethel to preach against segregation. He was active in community development and served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP. Bearden was elected the eighty-third bishop of the AME Church in 1964. He served as chair of the board of trustees of Morris Brown and was instrumental in helping the school achieve accreditation.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Basketball Player. A native of New Bern, North Carolina, and a graduate of Indiana University, Bellamy was a member of the 1960 U.S. Olympic gold medal basketball team. He started his professional career with the Chicago Packers, and in 1962, he was named National Basketball Association (NBA) Rookie of the Year. He was a four-time NBA All-Star player. Bellamy was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1993. In retirement, Bellamy was active with the NAACP, the Atlanta Urban League, and the YMCA. He also served on the board of directors of the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. Bennette was a graduate of Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. He played a crucial role in the leadership and organization of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC). He directed SCLC voter registration drives, and he was deputy director of the Georgia Voters League. He was the first director of the SCLC's Operation Bread Basket, a community project which engaged African American churches to challenge employment practices with the goal of desegregating workplaces. Bennette was one of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s closest and most trusted aides, and he served as advisor to Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter and to U. S. Ambassador Andrew Young when Young was mayor of Atlanta. Bennette was a member of the board of advisors and security director for The Martin Luther King Jr. Center for Non-Violent Social Change. Bennette's gravestone bears the motto "Commandante." Andrew Young wrote Bennette's epitaph: "You were always there when Martin needed you-ready to lay down your life for a friend. God has blessed you. Peace."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Nurse. Benning was a graduate of the Grady School of Nursing, and she earned a bachelor of science in nursing education from New York University. She served as supervisor of public health nurses for Atlanta and Fulton County and was an executive committee member of the National Nursing Association. Benning was an advocate for the education and professional recognition of African American nurses, and she founded the Atlanta School for Practical Nurse Education in 1963. A group of practical nurses who graduated only two weeks prior from Benning's school were among the professional nurses who served as flower ladies at her funeral. The Atlanta Chapter of the Grady Nurses Conclave, the Eula Benning Club, was named in her honor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Eula Benning.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Barber. During the Civil War. Moses Bentley was a body servant for his young slaveholder. He was at the battle of Manassas when the young man was killed, and he helped move the body from the battlefield. Bentley was appointed messenger of the Georgia House of Representatives in 1867. During a quarrel, he shot and killed African American legislator Malcolm Claiborne. Bentley was released on bond and later acquit ted. In 1879, he became captain of the Georgia Cadets, an African American military company. For many years, Bentley owned and operated a barbershop on Marietta Street.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Surgeon. In addition to his work as a physician, Dr. Billings was a director of Citizens Trust Bank, and he contributed greatly to the growth and expansion of Morris Brown College. He was associated with the Pineview Convalescent Center, and he founded the Atlanta Tailoring School for WWII veterans.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Accountant, Banker, Educator. Blayton, a WWI veteran, was a founder and secretary of the Pioneer Store Company in Oklahoma. In Atlanta, he was an auditor at Standard Life Insurance Company. He became the first African American certified public accountant (CPA) in Georgia in 1928. He opened an accounting firm, and he taught accounting and economics at Morehouse College, Atlanta University, and Morris Brown College. Blayton was a co-founder of the Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association, a significant financier of African American home loans, and he served as cashier and vice president for Citizens Trust Bank. In 1949, Blayton purchased WERD, the first radio station in the U. S. to be owned by African Americans. He was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A resident of Oklahoma like her husband, she received a teaching diploma from Langston University in Tulsa and taught in the Oklahoma public schools. She received her undergraduate degree from Morehouse College as part of a program for teachers and the wives of faculty members. She continued her studies at Atlanta University and New York University. She was a life member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA and a member of the League of Women Voters, the National Council of Negro Women, the Negro Women in Business clubs, and the National Association of Negro Business Women. She served as president of the Neighborhood Union from 1943 until 1950.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: He graduated from his parents' alma mater, Langston University, and earned his master's degree from Atlanta University. He worked as chief accountant in his father's firm and served as station manager at WERD for twenty years.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: An attorney, she taught business law at the Blayton College of Business and later served as president of the school with her mother in the role of vice president. She graduated with honors from both Spelman College and John Marshall Law School in Chicago, Illinois, and passed the bar in Illinois and Georgia. She practiced law in Atlanta and served as general counsel for Mutual Federal Savings and Loan.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Tuskegee Airman. An Atlanta native, Bohannon became fascinated with flying as a child by watching pilots take off and land at Candler field. He started his aviation career with civilian air training and a job as a carpenter's apprentice. He helped to construct Tuskegee Army Air Field (Moton Field) in Alabama. Bohannon graduated from the cadet training program in December 1944, but he did not get the opportunity to serve overseas. WWII ended, and Bohannon became an officer-pilot in the all African American 332nd Fighter Group stationed at Godman Field in Kentucky. After leaving the military, Bohannon headed the Southern Regional Commission's Georgia Veterans Service Project for African American service men. He also worked for the U. S. Post Office. He returned to Lincoln University where he had begun his studies years before and earned his degree in 1948. Bohannon worked for fifteen years in the Fulton County School System before becoming the first African American to hold the position of regional Management Training Officer with the U.S. Post Office. Bohannon later worked in the regional office of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. He took a leadership role in two community fundraising drives to erect statues in honor of Charles S. Harper, first principal of Booker T. Washington High School, and Joseph D. Winston of the Butler Street YMCA.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Civil Rights Leader, Politician, Scholar. While attending Morehouse College, Bond became a student protest leader, and in 1960 he helped organize the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). He served as SNCC's first communication director. Bond was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives in 1965 and later served in the Georgia Senate. At the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Illinois, he was spontaneously nominated as a vice presidential candidate, however, he was too young to hold office. Bond co-founded the Southern Poverty Law Center and served as its president. He was president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP before becoming chairman of the National NAACP. Bond was also a television commentator, newspaper columnist, poet, and college professor. His epitaph reads, "Easily Amused Race Man."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Father of Julian Bond. Bond senior was president of two historically black colleges-Fort Valley State College, where he was the first president, from 1939 to 1945, and Lincoln University, his alma mater, from 1945 to 1957. Bond Sr. was a noted social sciences researcher. Among other projects, he worked with C. Vann Woodward and John Hope Franklin conducting research for the NAACP's Legal Defense and Education Fund for the Supreme Court case of Brown v. Board of Education. Horace Bond served as dean of the school of education at Atlanta University from 1957 until shortly before his death in 1972.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Julia Washington attended Fisk University where she met Horace Bond, a faculty member. Bond discontinued her education while her husband served in various academic positions and studied to earn his PhD. At age fifty-six, she returned to school and earned a master of library science degree from Atlanta University. She worked for seven years at Atlanta University's Trevor Arnett Library and later served as a part-time reference librarian at the university's Robert W. Woodruff Library. She retired in 2000 at the age of ninety-two.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. A third-generation minister, Borders was pastor of Wheat Street Baptist Church from 1937 until 1988. Under his leadership, the church experienced the largest period of growth in its history. He was chair of a committee of adults who advised students during civil rights sit-ins in the 1960s. He was also a radio and television evangelist, and he used the media to promote support for civil rights activities. He married Julia Pate.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. She served as the director of Christian education at Wheat Street Baptist Church. She was president of the Atlanta Branch of the National Negro Women's Council, Inc. and a member of the board of directors for the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. A graduate of Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee, Bowden practiced medicine and operated a pharmacy in Griffin, Georgia, before moving his practice to Atlanta in 1922. He was a primary supporter of a nursery school in Griffin which bears his name. In Atlanta, Bowden's office was located on Auburn Avenue. A sports enthusiast, he was a hunter, golfer, and tennis player. He served as president of the Atlanta Tennis Club and sponsored various trophies in local sports to stimulate interest and competition. Bowden was a dedicated parishioner of St. Paul's Episcopal Church and was honored by the congregation for his role in financing the parish house-rectory. For his funeral, in lieu of flowers, family members requested that donations be made to St. Paul's building fund.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Priest. Father Bowden graduated from Morehouse College, in Atlanta, and General Theological Seminary and Columbia University, both in New York. He was ordained as a priest in 1929 and assumed the duties of rector of St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Atlanta in 1934. An army veteran, he served as chaplain of the Veterans Administration hospital in Tuskegee, Alabama, and in Montrose, New York. He was a life member of the NAACP and chairman of the board of directors for Fulton County, Georgia. He was a member of the Council on Aging and chairman of the board of directors for the Shepherd Center at Northside Hospital. Fulton County's multipurpose senior citizens center was named in his honor. He married Minnie Lee Perry.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Henry James Charles Bowden.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Theologian, Educator. Born enslaved, Bowen was the first African American to earn a PhD at Boston University in 1887. He began teaching historical theology at Gammon Theological Seminary in 1893 and was the first full-time African American professor at Gammon. Bowen was a supporter of African American intellectualism and an outspoken critic of racial injustice. At the 1895 Atlanta Cotton States and International Exposition, he served as secretary of a three-day conference on Africa and was a featured speaker on "Negro Day." In 1904, Bowen and journalist Max Barber founded The Voice of the Negro, a national literary magazine. Bowen served as president of Gammon from 1906 to 1910. He offered Gammon as shelter to hundreds of African Americans in September 1906 when thousands of white Americans rioted in the streets of Atlanta. He was head of the church history department until his retirement in 1926, but he continued to teach until 1932.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A former teacher of history and English at Tuskegee Institute, she was also proficient in Greek, Latin, and German. She was an accomplished vocalist and played both piano and organ. In 1895, she became professor of music at Clark College. She also served as president of the Georgia Women's Christian Temperance Union. Bowen married a second time to Irene Smallwood.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to John Wesley Edward Bowen.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Educator. Bowen grew up on the campus of Gammon Theological Seminary during his father's tenure at the school. He began his education at Clark College as a student in the kindergarten program. He later attended Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire. He earned an undergraduate degree, cum laude, from Wesleyan University in Middleton, Connecticut. After earning a master's degree at Harvard, he pastored various Methodist churches and taught at several schools in the South, including New Orleans University in Louisiana, Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, and Claflin College in South Carolina. He served overseas as a chaplain in WWI. Later, he was editor for the African American Central Jurisdiction's Christian Advocate, and in 1948 he was appointed bishop of the Atlantic Coast region of the Central Jurisdiction. For many years, he served as chairman of the Clark College board of trustees. He married Margaret Louise Davis.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. She was the president of Gilbert Academy, a highly regarded Methodist high school for African Americans in New Orleans. Ambassador Andrew Young was one of her students. She served as the first president of the Women's Society of Christian Service in the African American Central Jurisdiction of the Methodist Church, but her focus on race reform during her presidency had begun much earlier in life. In 1935, during her graduation ceremony at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio, she had refused to march in the processional-delaying the ceremony for an hour-until she was given her rightful place toward the front of the line. In Atlanta, she refused to shop at the city's segregated department stores and instead wore African clothing that she had purchased on her travels. She was also affiliated with the National Council of Negro Women, the League of Women Voters, Phyllis Wheatley YWCA, and Emory University School of Nursing. After the death of her husband, she erected a fountain in his memory on the Clark College campus. She had already established the Lelia Swanson Davis Meditation Room in Clark's Merner Hall in memory of her mother.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Brawley earned his bachelor's degree from Sam Houston College in Austin, Texas, and both his master's and doctoral degrees from Northwestern University. He served Clark College for sixty years, as dean from 1926 until 1941 and as president from 1941 until 1965. In 1941, Brawley coordinated the relocation of Clark from east Atlanta to the Atlanta University Center in southwest Atlanta. He also wrote The Clark College Legacy, a history of the school. The street where Clark's main administration building was located was named in his honor. Brawley served as president emeritus on the Clark College board of directors until his death. He married Georgia Williams.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A graduate of Atlanta University, she was a member of the Clark College faculty. She earned a master's degree in English from Iowa State University, and she was affiliated with the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Economist. Brazeal was a graduate of Morehouse College and earned his master's and doctoral degrees from Columbia University. He served Morehouse for more than forty years as professor, department chair, and dean. Brazeal wrote The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, Its Origin and Development, now a standard reference book in labor history, American economic history, and race relations. He served as president of the Association of Colleges and Secondary Schools and the National Association of Collegiate Deans and Registrars. He was affiliated with the American Economic Association, the American Academy of Political Science, the Southern Sociological Society, the Advisory Council of Academic Freedom Committee of the American Civil Liberties Union, and the NAACP. Brazeal was a member of the board of directors of Atlanta's Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association and the Southern Regional Council. He married Ernestine Erskine.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a Spelman graduate, faculty member, and alumnae secretary. She earned a master's degree from the University of Chicago.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Bryant became the pastor of Wheat Street Baptist Church in 1898. He was widely praised for his natural ability as an orator, and he drew large crowds that greatly increased the membership at Wheat Street from a few hundred to over 5,000. In 1904, he organized the Atlanta Benevolent Protective Association for the members of his congregation; the association was later acquired by Alonzo Herndon and was the precursor to the Atlanta Life Insurance Company. Bryant was a member of the NAACP and a leader in the Niagara Movement. He advocated for civil rights as part of his ministry. He was also chairman of the board of the Carrie Steele orphanage. When Atlanta's Great Fire of 1917 destroyed the church, Bryant's congregation built a new gothic revival style church with seating for 2,500. Bryant suffered a stroke in 1926 from which he never fully recovered. An Atlanta school was named in his honor. He married Sylvia Cecil Jenkins.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Church Worker. She organized, and served as the first president of, the Blue Triangle Center, later renamed the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA. She was active in the Baptist Convention and missionary society, and she was elected treasurer of the National Training School for Colored Girls located in Washington, D. C. In Atlanta, she was affiliated with the Anti-Tuberculosis Association. In 1909, she opened the Bryant Preparatory and Industrial Night School, later called the Sylvia Bryant Baptist Institute. She was the school's first president. She founded the school to provide training for working-class African American adults in "domestic science, practical industries, elementary branches, and the Bible." Courses included dressmaking, typing and shorthand, printing, and music. The institute also offered a day school for children.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Community Worker. Bugg was one of the nine founding members of the Neighborhood Union (NU). Bugg was one of the petitioners for the incorporation of the NU in 1911, and she was elected to the position of first-vice-president in 1915. Her husband was Jordan Bugg.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Jordan Bugg was a carpenter. He served on the "gentleman's committee" of the Neighborhood Union (NU), and he helped maintain the Neighborhood House, a community meeting place and help center sponsored by the NU.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Social Worker. Social service workers like Burch lived and worked in settlement houses in poor neighborhoods to provide services such as day care, education, and healthcare to the residents of the community. A graduate of Atlanta University, Burch was well known in Atlanta and highly regarded for her dedication to social service. For thirteen years, she held the trusted position of treasurer of the Gate City Free Kindergarten Association. The association operated five free kindergartens in Atlanta for African American children. One of the Gate City kindergartens was named in her honor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Chief of the Eastern Cherokee. Bushyhead was an American Indian chief from North Carolina who fought for the Confederate Army during the Civil War. At some point during his time in the military, he was reportedly promoted to Colonel and thus was called by that title after the war ended. In 1869, Bushyhead was elected council chairman which gave him the authority to represent the eastern Cherokees in Washington, D. C. Each Spring, Bushyhead traveled to Atlanta to solicit funds for his tribe. In May 1892, during his annual trip, he became gravely ill. He died in the African American boarding house where he had been staying and was buried at South-View by undertaker Mitchell Cargile. The news of Bushyhead's burial in an African American cemetery prompted local white Americans to suggest that funds be raised to move his body to the Confederate section of Oakland, the city cemetery. Whether Bushyhead was ever moved to Oakland, or returned to North Carolina, remains unknown.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Civil Rights Leader, City Councilman. Calhoun served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP and chairman of the NAACP Legal Redress Committee. He was once convicted of contempt when he refused a court order to turn over the Atlanta branch's financial records. He was also one of the co-founders of the Atlanta Negro Voters League. Calhoun was elected to the Atlanta City Council in 1973 at age seventy-four, and he introduced the resolution that created neighborhood planning units (NPUs) in the city. He worked with Economic Opportunity Atlanta on the model cities program and was a consultant with the Atlanta Regional Commission. Calhoun was also associated with the Butler Street YMCA. A lifelong learner, he earned a college degree from Morehouse College at age thirty-eight and a master's degree from Atlanta University at age sixty-nine.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Church Worker. Canady was a graduate of Clark College, a member of the AME church, and a minister's wife. She was at work in an office in the basement of Big Bethel when her clothes accidently caught fire. She ran from the building in a panic, but alert pedestrians rushed to help put out the flames. She was immediately taken to the hospital where her burns were dressed, and she was sent home. However, her condition worsened. She died of complications from her burns just a few days later. She married Hilliard D. Canady.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: He was a minister. Canady was a presiding elder in the AME church. He was born in Troup County, Georgia, in 1859, and he attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary in Atlanta and Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Son of Hilliard D. Canady. He was a physician. He also graduated from Meharry Medical College, and he opened a practice on Auburn Avenue. He was the medical inspector for African American public schools in Atlanta. He died of pneumonia nine months after his father's death.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Fraternal Leader. Cannon was a teacher and the founder of the Independent Benevolent Order.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Carpenter, Undertaker. Cargile was the first African American undertaker listed in the Atlanta city directory.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Scholar, Author. Carter was pastor of Friendship Baptist Church for more than sixty years.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Church and Temperance Worker. As First Lady of Friendship Baptist Church, she organized a chapter of the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU)for her congregation. She was later elected treasurer of the Georgia Women's Christian Temperance Union. The WCTU promoted temperance and clean living among the city's African American poor. Members raised funds to aid poor families, visited the sick, and distributed literature to prisoners in Atlanta's chain gang. Carter was a WCTU superintendent of prison and jail work and assistant superintendent of evangelistic work. She was the wife of Edward R. Carter and the mother of Raymond Holmes Carter.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. A graduate of Morehouse College, R.H. Carter was an eye, ear, nose, and throat specialist. He served as a doctor-soldier in WWI. He was also a commissioner of the Boy Scouts of America and president of the local scouting club. He was a member of the Atlanta Medical Association and served as president of the Georgia Medical Association. He was affiliated with Morehouse College.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician, Educator. Carver was a jazz flutist and professor of music at Clark College, his alma mater. He gained his first professional experience performing with Atlanta band leader J. Neal Montgomery. In the early 1930s, Carver recorded with famous band leaders such as Dave Nelson, Spike Hughes, and Benny Carter. Carver also played saxophone and flute with drummer Chick Webb's orchestra. After Webb died, Ella Fitzgerald took over the Webb orchestra, and Carver continued to play with the group for a time. In 1942, Carver joined the Clark College faculty. He directed the concert and marching bands, and he wrote the music to Clark's fight song, "Hail Roaring Panther." During his undergraduate years at Clark, he organized a band with fellow students called the "Collegiate Ramblers" or sometimes, "The Collegians." Carver earned a master's degree in music education from VanderCook College of Music in Chicago, Illinois, in 1952. Under the administration of Jessie M. Wartman, music supervisor of Atlanta's elementary schools for African Americans, Carver organized the first elementary school bands. Though he was not the first to play jazz on the flute, many jazz historians give Carver credit for being the first "true" jazz flutist. He married Savannah Joyce Sinkler.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Author. A reading specialist, she was the author of several published poems and a popular 1980s book for children, "Johnny Lincoln and his Three Dogs." She graduated from Clark College and earned a master's degree from Atlanta University. She earned a reading specialist degree from the University of Georgia.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Librarian, Social Activist. Cary was born in Indiana and received her early education in Michigan. A graduate of Wilberforce University in Ohio, she later taught in Wilberforce's foreign languages department. She married AME minister Rev. Jefferson Cary, a trustee at Wilberforce. In 1900, she helped organize the first free kindergarten for Atlanta's African American children. She also served as a teacher and principal of the high school department at Morris Brown College and chair of Morris Brown's English department. Cary worked with W. E. B. Du Bois and others to help open a public library in Atlanta for African Americans. In 1921, she was named the first librarian of the Auburn Avenue Branch of the Atlanta Public Library. She was the daughter of John R. Dugged, a harness maker and teacher.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A graduate of Spelman College, she earned her master's degree at Atlanta University. She taught for several years at Bell Street Elementary School and served as principal of the E. P. Johnson and Wesley Avenue elementary schools. She was a member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA and a supporter of the Girl Scouts. An Atlanta public school was named in her honor. She married Josephus Roosevelt Coan.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Missionary, Educator. He was an AME church pastor, teacher, and missionary. Coan graduated from Howard University and Yale Divinity School, and he earned a PhD from the Hartford Seminary Foundation. Coan was the college minister at Morris Brown College. He was chair of Morris Brown's philosophy department for twenty years. He also served as a missionary in Southern and Central Africa, and he served as acting bishop presiding over South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Botswana, Namibia, and Malawi. Coan was one of the original faculty members at the Interdenominational Theological Center where he spent nineteen years.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Community Volunteer. Connally graduated from Atlanta University and Atlanta's School of Social Work. She was a school teacher and a member of various community organizations. She was president of the Neighborhood Union from 1937 until 1942. Connally organized the Mother's Club of Boy Scout Troop 90, the first African American Boy Scout troop in Atlanta and the first African American troop to attend a World Scout Jamboree.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Artist, Musician, Railway Worker. Cooke was a self-taught artist. Beginning in 1917, his editorial cartoons were a regular feature in the Atlanta Independent newspaper. Cooke was also a talented jazz musician and band leader. In 1937, he helped organize the first musicians' union for African Americans in Georgia, the Atlanta Musicians' Protective Association. Soon after its founding, the union became affiliated with the American Federation of Musicians as Local 462. Cooke served as secretary-treasurer of the organization and represented the group as a delegate at national conventions. Cooke worked as a messenger for the Southern Railway Company for sixty-three years.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Dentist. Cooper graduated from Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee. A native Georgian, he started his dental practice in Atlanta with a business loan from Citizens Trust Bank. In 1954, Cooper was elected president of the Georgia Dental Society. He also belonged to the National Dental Association. He married Ann Louise Nixon.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She worked as a secretary and policy writer for Atlanta Life Insurance Company until the birth of her first child. Afterwards, she became involved in civic work and served as president of the board of directors of the Gate City Day Nursery Association, an outgrowth of the Gate City Free Kindergarten Association. She was a charter member of the Atlanta chapter of The Links, Inc., a nationwide community service organization of African American women. She founded the Grady Homes Girls Club Guild, an auxiliary organization of adult supporters of the Girls Club, and in 1939, she co-founded the first African American Cub Scout troop in Atlanta. At age 106, Ann Cooper was one of the oldest persons to vote in the 2008 U. S. presidential election. Cooper gained nationwide attention when president-elect Barack Obama called to thank her for her vote and paid tribute to her in his victory speech on election night. Cooper first registered to vote in 1941 but deferred exercising that right for many years, depending instead upon her husband to vote on behalf on the household. Her memoir, A Century and Some Change: My Life Before the President Called My Name, co-authored with Karen Grigsby Bates, was published in January 2010.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. A native of Alabama, she married shoemaker John Wesley Cox (d. 1893). They came to Atlanta in 1872. In 1900, she founded the Cox Brothers Funeral Home with two of her sons, Allen and Charles S. Cox.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Son of Emily Griffin Cox. In 1900, he and his brother Charles S. Cox joined their mother in founding the Cox Brothers Funeral Home in Atlanta.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Insurance Agent, Civic and Religious Worker. Craddock worked as a mailman for many years before becoming an agent for the Pilgrim Health and Life Insurance Company. He served as a deacon of Antioch Baptist Church and as superintendent of the Sunday school. He was also active in religious and civic affairs, and he was a gifted orator. In later years, Craddock was also associated with Friendship Baptist Church. Craddock lived on Gray Street, and as a child he attended the Gray Street Elementary School. The school was later renamed in his memory for his many contributions to the school and its students. He married Lizzie Chapman.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a Spelman College graduate and one of the founders of the Helping Hand Club, an organization dedicated to serving the needy.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Author. Born a free man on St. Martin's Island in the British West Indies, Crogman began traveling the world as a sailor while still a teenager. His travels took him to Europe, Asia, and South America. In the United States, he attended Pierce Academy in Massachusetts and proved himself a gifted student. Crogman taught English for three years at Claflin University, a school started by the Freedman's Aid Society in Orangeburg, South Carolina. He later pursued a degree in classical studies at Atlanta University. He joined the faculty of Clark College but also continued his formal education, and in 1879, he received a master's degree from Atlanta University. He received doctoral degrees from both Atlanta University and Clark College in 1901. After twenty-five years as a professor of classics, in 1903, Crogman was appointed Clark College's first African American president. Crogman also served as secretary of the trustee boards of both Clark College and Gammon Theological Seminary. Crogman was the author of several books, and he was one of the first African Americans to be included in Who's Who of America. He married Lavinia C. Mott.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A native of Charlotte, North Carolina, she was also a graduate of Atlanta University. She had been ill for several months before the death of her husband, and she died a few days following him. A double funeral was held for them in Crogman Chapel at Clark College.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. A native of Monticello, Georgia, Crolley was born enslaved, and when his slaveholder joined the army during the Civil War, he took Crolley with him. During slavery, Crolley had been trained by his father as a blacksmith. After emancipation, he continued to work as a blacksmith while attending school. He completed an undergraduate degree at Lincoln University and entered the ministry. In 1874, Crolley organized the first congregation of Warren Memorial United Methodist Church in Atlanta. Crolley married Mary Willis Cobb.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was the sister of Luther Judson Price. She was born enslaved in McDonough, Georgia, and she was sold on the auction block, for the first time, when she was only five years old. As an adult, she was active in relief and prison work in Georgia's jails, prison camps, and chain gangs. For over forty years, she aided incarcerated men and women, regardless of race. She frequently visited the inmates and distributed religious literature. She also aided prisoners in locating and communicating with family members.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Entrepreneur. While still a teen, Cunningham left her hometown of Fitzgerald, Georgia, to join the Silas Green Show, one of the nation's largest traveling vaudeville troupes. By the 1930s, she had married James Cunningham and settled in Atlanta. She operated two hotels, the Reid House on Decatur Street, managed by her husband, and another on Central Avenue where she kept an apartment. Cunningham admittedly tolerated her husband's marital infidelity, but in 1936, a jealous lover, a resident of the Reid House, attacked and slashed him in the shoulder with a knife. He was rushed to Grady Hospital but died an hour later from blood loss. Cunningham hired prominent white American attorney William Schley Howard to aid the state in prosecuting her husband's attacker. The accused woman, who insisted that she had not intended murder, was convicted and sentenced to a nine-year jail term, rather than the death penalty sought by the state. On New Year's Day in 1941, Cunningham opened the Hotel Royal, a modern fifty-room hotel on Auburn Avenue. The hotel provided much needed lodging for African American visitors who were not allowed in Atlanta's whites-only hotels. In 1949, Cunningham expanded her business and opened the Royal Peacock Club in the space that had formerly housed the Top Hat Club. The popular Top Hat Club opened in 1937 and operated for twelve years under the ownership of Jesse B. Blayton, Lorimer Milton, and Clayton Yates.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Caterer. A resident of Atlanta for forty years, Daniels gained nationwide fame for her catering expertise. Though she was already a skilled professional with a growing reputation, she attended cooking schools in New York and Boston to continue refining her methods. Among her most famous clientele were Andrew Carnegie and four U.S. presidents. Following a meal catered by Daniels, First Lady Florence Harding exclaimed enthusiastically that Daniels should come to the White House to "show our chef just how to do it." Daniels' largest catering job was a luncheon for 16,000 at Agnes Scott College. Daniels was a member of the Atlanta Civic and Political League. She participated in the religious, social, and civic life of her community, especially in the area of child welfare and education. She served as president of the Atlanta Parent-Teachers Council and treasurer of the National Congress of Parents and Teachers. She was also a trustee of the Leonard Street Orphans Home and a member of the Women's Republican Advisory Committee. Upon her death, community members established the Willie Daniels Memorial Fund for Children.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Newspaper Editor, Fraternal and Political Leader. Davis was editor and publisher of the Atlanta Independent and head of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows. Davis married Jimmie W. Porter.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A native of Dawson, Georgia, she attended the Hampton and Tuskegee institutes. She was a member of the Women's Republican Advisory Committee.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Davison attended Atlanta University. When he moved to Fort Valley, Georgia, he began teaching students in his home. He saw the need for a larger, more formal educational approach and in 1895, he founded the Fort Valley High and Industrial School for African Americans. The school was chartered as a public school by Houston County in early 1896. In its early years, Davison mortgaged his home and farm to finance the school. A devastating fire damaged the main school building in 1902 and created more financial hardship. Davison's desire to include liberal arts and teacher training in the school's curriculum was not shared by the school's funders, and the board of trustees dismissed Davison from his role as principal in 1903. In later years, the school began to move toward Davison's original vision. A teacher training program was introduced in 1929, and in 1939, the school merged with the State Teachers and Agricultural College of Forsyth to become Fort Valley State College.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Carpenter, Preacher, Folk Philosopher. Writer Frank L. Stanton incorporated Patrick Dickey's clever common-sense philosophy as a regular feature of his Atlanta Constitution column, "Just from Georgia." Known as "Brother Dickey" to the readers of Stanton's column, Patrick Dickey was born enslaved in Virginia around 1830. He came to Atlanta in the mid-1880s. Stanton's column brought Dickey local fame for his pragmatic, often humorous, philosophical reflections on life and morality. He worked as a carpenter and was a self-made preacher-though not a church member. Upon his death, the Atlanta Constitution called him "The Sable Sage," but Dickey died a pauper. His body was placed in a simple pine board coffin; no funeral service was held for him.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Postal Worker, Fraternal Leader. Dobbs was a well-known civic and political leader. He married Irene Ophelia Thompson.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a native of Columbus, Mississippi. She chaired the deaconess board of the First Congregational Church. She also served on the board of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA. A scholarship was established in her memory at Spelman College, the alma mater of all six of her daughters.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Opera Singer. Dobbs was a coloratura soprano who received her first serious vocal study as an undergraduate at Spelman College. Dobbs continued with advanced music studies in New York and Paris. She graduated first in her Spelman class with majors in Spanish and music. She also earned a master's degree in Spanish from Columbia University Teachers College. In 1951, she won first prize in the Geneva International Music Competition, and in 1953, she became the first African American to sing a principal role at the La Scala Opera House in Milan, Italy. In 1956, Dobbs made her debut at the New York Metropolitan Opera Company. She was the first African American woman to be offered a long-term contract with the Met. She was married twice-first to Spanish playwright and journalist, Luis Rodriguez, who died a year into their marriage, then to Swedish journalist Bengt Janzon who predeceased her in 1997. She was the daughter of John Wesley and Irene Thompson Dobbs.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. Douthard, an Alabama native, was the first African American doctor to open an office in Decatur, Georgia. He did not finish his high school education until age twenty-five, but a year later, with only fifty cents in his pocket, he began his medical education at Leonard Medical School at Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina. In addition to his medical practice, Douthard was active in civic, church, and fraternal organizations. He was a charter member of the Atlanta Medical Association and served as president of the organization for three years. He was also a member of the National Medical Association. Douthard held executive positions in two of Atlanta's private hospitals for African Americans: Mercy Hospital and Dunbar Hospital. He married Beatrice Estelle Hubert.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A native of Hancock County, Georgia, she was a graduate of Spelman College. She taught at various colleges and schools during her teaching career, including Anniston Normal and Industrial College in Anniston, Alabama; Arkansas Baptist college in Little Rock, Arkansas; and the Atlanta Public Schools. In Atlanta, she was principal of Mayson Avenue School.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Known as "Baby Drake" to the citizens of Atlanta, two-month-old Elaine Drake was diagnosed with miliary tuberculosis and meningitis. The prescribed treatment was streptomycin, a rare and expensive drug in 1947 which her parents could not afford. C. A. Scott of the Atlanta Daily World newspaper started a fund to provide the drug for Baby Drake. News came of the baby's death just a week after the funding drive began. A planned benefit performance at the Top Hat Club was cancelled, and the money already raised was used for the baby's hospital and funeral expenses. The remaining amount was designated for a "sick baby" fund to more quickly aid children like Baby Drake in the future.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Missionary. Drummer worked to pay her way through Clark College and graduated in 1901. She trained as a nurse-deaconess at the New England Deaconess Training College in Boston, Massachusetts, and graduated from that institution in 1904. Drummer spent sixteen years in the Women's Foreign Missionary Society, Pacific Branch, in Angola, Africa. On regular trips home to the U. S., she inspired audiences through numerous speaking engagements. Illness finally forced her permanent return to the U.S. For her funeral, in lieu of flowers, she had requested contributions for books for Africa. Drummer left half of her estate to the Women's Foreign Missionary Society.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Druggist. Drummond was born in Kingston, Jamaica. He was founder of the Progressive Spiritualist church and schools in Atlanta and president of the National Psychic Science Alliance. He established schools and churches in Havana, Cuba, and in the U. S. in Miami, Florida; Dayton, Ohio; and Chicago, Illinois. Hiram O'Neal started his spiritual training with Drummond. Drummond was also a member of the Atlanta Civic and Political League and the Butler Street YMCA.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Deputy Surveyor of Customs. Easley, a free person of color, was about ten years old when the Civil War ended. He and his family had lived for a time in Atlanta during the war, but they were forced to flee when Sherman's troops advanced upon the city. After the war ended, Easley learned to read and write while working as an office boy in a law firm. He returned to Atlanta where he attended the Storrs school. He worked as a waiter and later became a postal railway clerk. He was appointed Deputy Surveyor of Customs under C. C. Cater. Easley was active in politics, and in 1884, he served as secretary of the Georgia Republican convention in Atlanta. He also served as Grand Chief of the State Grand Lodge of Good Samaritans. Easley was a persuasive orator and a skillful writer. His articles were published in various religious and secular periodicals, including the Atlanta Defiance newspaper. Easley was associated with the Abyssinian Library, a subscription reading room established in 1880 for African Americans in Atlanta.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Ellis was pastor of Paradise (Reed Street) Baptist Church from 1933 until his death. A graduate of Morehouse College School of Religion, he was awarded the doctorate of divinity by Selma University. Ellis founded the Chariot Wheels gospel radio program which aired on Atlanta station WSB. He was president of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers Union and a member of the board of the National Baptist Convention. He married Vashti Elizabeth Calanthe Scott.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Journalist. A member of the Atlanta Daily World Scott publishing family, she authored the "Eleanor" column which featured advice for the lovelorn, and ''Majoring with Minors," a column on child rearing.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Finley was the first Spelman graduate to earn an advanced degree from Atlanta University. As principal of the Yonge Street School, she helped organize the first African American parent-teacher association in the United States in 1911, and she served as the group's corresponding secretary. Finley was treasurer of the Gate City Teachers Association, a predominantly African American organization. She and other members challenged the Atlanta Board of Education on the issue of salary discrimination. She was a member of the Atlanta Citizens Committee, a field worker for the NAACP, and she served on the first board of directors of the Atlanta Urban League. Finley also organized a night school for African Americans in Atlanta. After retiring from the Atlanta Public Schools, she led the department of education at Alabama State University.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Fisher, a free person of color born in Baltimore, Maryland, was a presiding elder of the Methodist Episcopal Church. In 1852, Fisher was a delegate to a convention of free people of color in Maryland. The convention focused on issues of emigration to Liberia and education for African American children. In Atlanta, Fisher was pastor of the Loyd Street Methodist Episcopal Church. Fisher's grave marker was "erected by the Brethren of his conference." The inscription on the marker also acknowledges his wife: "Beside him sleeps his faithful Gaddy, the loving and helpful companion of his life."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Poet, Artist, Editor, Minister. Flanagan's articles and poetry appeared in the Atlanta Independent, Atlanta Daily World, and Atlanta Constitution newspapers. As early as 1913, The Macon Telegraph also published Flanagan's poems for a regular feature called ''Verses Over Night." Flanagan worked for the U. S. Postal Railway Service for thirty-three years while pursuing his writing career. He was born in Lumpkin County, Georgia, and much of his subject matter came from his experience of growing up in rural Georgia. His father, Monroe Sanford Flanagan, a farmer by profession, was also a songwriter. In 1926, Flanagan solicited the help of established scholar and author W. E. B. Du Bois. Flanagan revealed that he was experiencing difficulties finding funding for the publication of his work, but a year later, The Atlanta Independent published a limited edition of a collection of Flanagan's poems and offered the book at a discount to the newspaper's subscribers. For many years, the Atlanta Daily World featured Flanagan's poems in his popular column, "Up from Georgia with my Banjo." In addition to his newspaper work, he was well known for his published poetry collections, By the Pine Knot Torches, The Road to Mount McKeithan, and The Canyons at Providence. Georgia's first poet laureate, Frank L. Stanton, and Georgia state historian Lucian Lamar Knight wrote introductions for Flanagan's books.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: He graduated from Morehouse College. As an officer in the U.S. Air Force, Robert Flanagan engaged African American military personnel in support of the Civil Rights Movement. He served as executive secretary of the Atlanta Branch of the NAACP from 1967 to 1968 and as field services director from 1968 to 1978. In 1978, he was elected president of the NAACP Georgia Conference of Branches and served in that position until 1984.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Educator. A native Atlantan and a graduate of Atlanta University, Flipper served the AME Church as pastor, presiding elder, and bishop. In Atlanta, he pastored Allen Temple, Big Bethel, and St. Paul. Flipper Temple and other AME churches were named in his honor. Flipper became dean of Morris Brown College in 1904, then president, but he left the college in 1908 to assume the role of bishop. Flipper received his doctor of divinity degree from Allen University in South Carolina; the library at Allen University was named in his honor. Flipper also received a doctor of laws degree from Wilberforce University in Ohio.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: The first wife of Bishop Joseph Simeon Flipper, she was honored in 1921 by the naming of an Atlanta church in her memory, Amanda Flipper Memorial Temple.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: The second wife of Bishop Joseph Simeon Flipper, she was a teacher at Morris Brown. She served as president of the Women's Home and Foreign Missionary Society in the Atlanta AME conference.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: The third wife of Bishop Joseph Simeon Flipper, she was a teacher at the Forsyth Agricultural and Industrial College in Forsyth, Georgia. She also taught at Morris Brown. She served as state president of the South Carolina Mission program while Flipper was the presiding bishop in South Carolina. Bishop Flipper was the brother of Henry O. Flipper, the first African American graduate of the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Educator. Fountain was the fifth president of Morris Brown College, from 1911 until 1920, and a bishop in the AME Church, from 1920 until his retirement in 1952. He received degrees from Morris Brown and Turner Theological Seminary, Northwestern University in Illinois, and Central University in Indiana. He was first licensed to preach in 1892 in his home town of Elberton, Georgia, and he pastored a number of churches-building, organizing, improving, remodeling, and paying off their mortgages. In Atlanta, he pastored Allen Temple. In addition to his many church leadership roles and affiliations, Fountain was a member of the Interracial Commission of Georgia, National Negro Business League, NAACP, and Butler Street YMCA. Fountain Hall, originally Atlanta University's Stone Hall, was built by noted Swedish-born architect Gottfried Norrman. Stone Hall was renamed when Morris Brown College moved to Atlanta University's former campus and began using the building for its academic offices. Fountain Hall was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1975, but in 2010 the building was listed as one of Georgia's Places in Peril by the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Fountain was the seventh president of Morris Brown College. In the early years of his administration, his father, Morris Brown's fifth president, served the college as chancellor. Fountain and his father led the college through the Great Depression. They declared bankruptcy and formed a corporation to keep the school operating, and the younger Fountain chose to take no salary during the financial crisis. His tenure as president ended in controversy over a charge regarding the misappropriation of funds. After leaving Morris Brown, he served as secretary-treasurer of the General Board of Education of the AME Church.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Restaurant Owner. Jones started her first restaurant, the Evelyn Jones Cafe, in 1936. In the 1940s, she and her husband Luther Ellis Frazier expanded the business and renamed it Frazier's Cafe Society. The Auburn Avenue restaurant was a popular meeting place for African American civic, political, and religious organizations in Atlanta, especially during the years of the Civil Rights Movement when patrons included Benjamin Mays, Martin Luther King Jr., and Thurgood Marshall. Frazier was a member of the Republican party, and she was affiliated with the Association of Negro Business and Professional Women's Clubs, Morris Brown College, and the NAACP.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: In the 1940s, he and his wife, Evelyn Jones Frazier, expanded her Evelyn Jones Cafe and renamed it Frazier's Cafe Society, a popular Auburn Avenue meeting place during the Civil Rights Movement.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Fuller founded the Fire Baptized Holiness Church of God of the Americas. At the time of his death, he presided as bishop over 800 churches in the U.S., England, British West Indies, and Virgin Islands. His funeral was held at Big Bethel AME Church, and the sanctuary was filled to overflowing. His funeral service lasted more than five hours. The highway in front of the church's headquarters in Greenville has been renamed in his memory. The Fuller Normal Industrial Institute, established by Bishop Fuller in Atlanta in 1912, moved to Toccoa, Georgia, in 1913, then to Greenville, South Carolina, in 1923.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
