people.biography: A Meharry Medical College graduate, Funderburg practiced medicine in Jasper and Putnam counties in Georgia. In 1938, a flu outbreak in Putnam took the life of the only white American doctor in the area. Funderburg won the confidence of white Americans in both counties when he was forced to single-handedly manage the epidemic. Funderburg was appointed by President Dwight Eisenhower to the Georgia Committee of the U.S. Civil Rights Commission, and he was a participant in the White House Conference on Civil Rights during the administration of President Lyndon Johnson. Funderburg was a founding member of the North Georgia Medical Association. He married Ethel Maud Westmoreland.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a graduate of Atlanta University and one of the organizers and supporters of the Jasper County Training School.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Banker. Son of Frederick Douglass and Ethel Maud Westmoreland Funderburg. Funderburg was the first African American to earn a degree from the graduate school of banking at Rutgers University. He served Citizens Trust Bank as president and chief executive officer. Funderburg directed the expansion and technical modernization of the bank's operations while focusing the institution on funding commercial projects that would improve the quality of life in Atlanta's neighborhoods. At the time of Funderburg's retirement in 1992, Citizens Trust was the second-largest bank in the nation owned by African Americans. Funderburg owned a twenty-three-acre farm where he raised quarter horses. He also tended a large vegetable garden at the farm and was known among friends for his excellent cooking skills.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A graduate of Clark College, Gideons received his master's degree at Atlanta University. He was cashier of the Standard Life Insurance Company in North Carolina prior to working for the Atlanta Life Insurance Company. He first served as principal of the evening program at Booker T. Washington High School then was appointed principal of the David T. Howard school in 1944. At the time of his death, Gideons was the supervising principal of extension, vocational, and adult personnel for Atlanta's African American public schools. An Atlanta public school was named in his honor. He married Jannette Woods.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. She was a teacher in the DeKalb County public schools for more than twenty-five years.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Philosopher, Scholar-Activist. A graduate of Talladega College, Golightly earned his MA and PhD degrees in philosophy from the University of Michigan. Golightly, a Rosenwald Fellow, was appointed professor at Olivet College in Michigan in 1945. Five years later, limitations placed upon their academic freedom caused Golightly and his first wife, Catherine Cater, also a Rosenwald Fellow and an English professor at Olivet, to resign in protest. Golightly then became the first African American to teach philosophy at the University of Wisconsin. He was the first African American to serve on the Milwaukee School Board. In 1969, he became dean of the College of Arts at Michigan's Wayne State University. Golightly served as the first African American president of the Detroit School Board, and he was credited with being a principal influence in the peaceful desegregation of Detroit's public schools. He donated his body to University of Michigan Medical School, and a cenotaph was placed for him at South-View.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Community Leader, Journalist. Greenlea was co-founder and president of the Summerhill Neighborhood Inc., a community development corporation. Greenlea Commons, a seventy-six-unit town home development in Summerhill was named in his honor. He graduated from Morehouse College and earned a master's degree from Atlanta University. He served for twenty years as executive director of the Atlanta NAACP. He was an editor at the Atlanta Daily World, and he worked for Economic Opportunity Atlanta.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Singer. Guest was an original member of the Pips, later known as Gladys Knight and the Pips. The group won Grammy awards in 1973 and 1988. In 1996, they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. They were also recognized with a lifetime achievement award by the Rhythm and Blues Foundation. When Gladys Knight left the group, Guest co-founded a music production company. Later, he started Crew Records. In 2013, he published his autobiography, Midnight Train from Georgia: A Pip's Journey. Guest's sister, Eleanor Perry, was also an original member of the Pips.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Carpenter, Building Contractor. According to Atlanta historian Edward R. Carter, Hamilton served in the Union Army during the Civil War, was elected to the city council of Eufaula, Alabama, and served two terms in Alabama's Reconstruction Legislature. Hamilton built many fine homes in Eufaula, including his own. He was given a gold watch and a piece of property by the city of Eufaula for the part he played in preventing a fire and robbery secretly being plotted by African Americans. By 1876, Hamilton had moved his family to Atlanta and started the construction company of Alexander Hamilton and Son. Hamilton's obituary in the Atlanta Constitution on May 27, 1911, noted that "some of the best-known buildings in Atlanta were erected by him." Two of those structures included the Good Samaritan building on Ivy Street and the Linton Hopkins House in Ansley Park. Hamilton also built many of the large houses on Peachtree and Washington streets. He worked as superintendent at W. L. Trainer & Company for several years, and he also was the contractor for Morris Brown College. Hamilton was one of the organizers of the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company and a member of the National Negro Business League. Hamilton built his Atlanta home on Hilliard street where for three generations family members continued to reside.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Politician, Activist. Hamilton was the first African-American woman in the deep South to be elected as a state legislator. An Atlanta native, Hamilton graduated from Atlanta University and earned a master's degree from Ohio State University. She taught psychology at Clark College, Atlanta University, and Le Moyne Junior College in Memphis, Tennessee. In 1943, she was appointed the first female executive director of the Atlanta Urban League. In a special election in 1965, Hamilton and seven other African Americans were elected to the Georgia legislature. Until then, no African American had served in the Georgia legislature since Reconstruction. Hamilton served in the Georgia senate until 1984. She was a principal architect of the 1973 Atlanta city charter which brought African-Americans onto the Atlanta City Council in proportion to their percentage of the population. After her service in the legislature, she was an advisor to the U. S. Civil Rights Commission. Atlanta's Emory University annually hosts the Grace Towns Hamilton lecture. In 2006, Hamilton was named a Georgia Woman of Achievement. She was the daughter of George Towns and Nellie McNair. She married Henry Cooke Hamilton.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Hamilton was a native of Atlanta and a graduate of Atlanta University. He earned a master's degree from the University of Pittsburgh and a doctorate from the University of Cincinnati. He worked at Le Moyne Junior College in Memphis as dean, registrar, and professor of education. In Atlanta, he served as principal of Atlanta University's high school and taught at Morehouse College and Atlanta University. He also served as dean of Morehouse. He was a member of the NAACP and the Urban League. His grandfather was well-known building contractor Alexander Hamilton.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Singer. Hamilton, an Atlanta native, was a contralto soloist. During WWII, Hamilton served in the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps (WAAC) as a jeep driver, but when her musical talents were discovered, she began performing with the WAAC Band. She married Atlanta singer Henry Ellison, and the two performed separately and together in Atlanta, Boston, throughout the East, and in the Midwest. When the couple moved to Boston, she continued her musical studies. While she sang primarily sacred music and spirituals, and performed mainly for church audiences, her repertoire also included classical and popular pieces. Hamilton performed with Arthur Fiedler and the Boston Pops and toured France with the Patterson Chorale. She performed at numerous Boston venues- Jordan Hall, the Gardner Museum, and John Hancock Hall. She was also the first African American to appear as a soloist in Boston's Freedom Hall. She frequently performed concerts for the peace and social justice movements, including the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom. The city of Boston awarded her the Sacco-Vanzetti Memorial Award for her contributions to social justice.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner. Harden was the first African American to own and operate a gas station in Atlanta. The Harden Service Station at 44 Hunter Street opened about 1930; he purchased a second station on Auburn Avenue in 1935. A twenty-four hour business operator, Harden closed only once in thirty years-on the day that U. S. President John Kennedy was assassinated. He married Willie Lee "Billie" Harden.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She and her husband, John Harden, co-owned and managed the Atlanta Black Crackers baseball team. There was no eulogy at her funeral because Harden believed she delivered her own eulogy in the way she lived her life.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Harper was the first principal of Booker T. Washington High School, the first public junior/senior high school for African Americans in Atlanta. A graduate of Morris Brown College, Harper taught in Hancock, Bartow, and Henry county schools in Georgia. In Atlanta, before being appointed principal at Washington High, he was the first principal of Morris Brown's high school department and first principal of the Yonge Street evening school. Harper served as executive secretary of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association, a professional organization for African American teachers. He also served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP. He married Carrie Belle Nichols.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Baseball Player. An Atlanta native, Harper was an outfielder noted for his speed in racing to catch the ball. He played for the Atlanta Black Crackers, Philadelphia Stars, Cincinnati Clowns, Kansas City Monarchs, and Birmingham Black Barons. Harper (nicknamed "Rough House") played football at Atlanta's Booker T. Washington High School in the early 1940s. At that time, Washington High did not have a baseball team, but Harper had the opportunity to play both football and baseball when he enrolled at Clark College. After his professional baseball career ended, Harper worked for the Chrysler Corporation in Detroit, Michigan, where he served as athletics director for the employee union.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician, Educator. Harreld was a concert violinist and director of the music departments in the Atlanta University System. He also played piano, organ, and flute. Harreld was one of the founders of the National Association of Negro Musicians. He studied at Chicago Musical College, Frederick Music College, and the Stern Conservatory of Music in Berlin, Germany. As a private teacher, Harreld influenced and nurtured young musicians throughout Atlanta. He also founded glee clubs at Morehouse and Spelman colleges. Morehouse Glee Club members provided the music and served as pallbearers at his funeral. He married Claudia T. White.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was Spelman's first college graduate and daughter of Morehouse College founder, Rev. William Jefferson White. She taught German and Latin at Spelman and Morehouse Colleges. She served as director of the Gate City Day Nursery Association for two decades. A dormitory at Spelman was named in her memory.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. She was the first living African American female for whom DeKalb County named a public school. Harris began her teaching career in 1939 and taught in various school systems before coming to DeKalb County. She was a Jeanes Supervisor, one of a group of advocates who worked to improve education for African American communities from 1908 to 1968. Many Jeanes Supervisors were affiliated with the NAACP, and thus they were also advocates for voting rights and leaders in the early Civil Rights Movement. From the 1940s to the 1980s, Harris served as an instructional coordinator and PTA organizer.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.full_name: Phoebe Lucille Fraser Burney Callier Hart
people.biography: Educator. Hart served as dean of women at Clark College for many years. An Alabama native and graduate of Clark College, she earned a master's degree from Gammon Theological Seminary. She served as director of religious education for the southeast district of Congregational churches and was administrative secretary to Benjamin Mays at Morehouse College. She married Atlanta physician John Wesley Burney, then married again to physician Napoleon Bonaparte Callier of Chattanooga, Tennessee. In Chattanooga, she was assistant to the president of Zion College. Hart sponsored two African children and brought them to the U. S.-her "sons" John Pratt and Daniel Anom. She married a third time to Clarence C. Hart.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: He opened a plumbing business on Auburn Avenue in 1925. That same year he invested $100 to help establish Mutual Federal Building and Loan Association. Hart and other founders of Mutual Federal initially gathered at the Butler Street YMCA to discuss the idea of providing financing to African Americans when white-owned institutions would not lend to them. By the 1990s, Mutual Federal was one of the leading African American companies in the nation.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
people.spouse: Phoebe Lucille Fraser Burney Callier Hart

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. In 1929, she opened the Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Entrepreneur. In 1950, Henderson became the first African American to earn a master's degree in fashion merchandising from New York University. In Atlanta, she owned a fashion design business and dress shop, and she taught at Spelman College and Atlanta University. Henderson was a fashion editor and nationally syndicated columnist for the Associated Negro Press. After traveling to her first fashion show in Europe in 1954, she founded Henderson Travel Services, Inc. with her husband, civic and business leader Jacob Robert Henderson.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Henderson Travel was the first African American travel agency in the Southeast and the first accredited African American travel agency in the nation. Henderson Travel arranged trips for notable civil rights leaders Andrew Young and Martin Luther King Jr., and at a time when commercial airlines did not fly to the African continent, Henderson Travel provided charter tours to West African countries.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Realtist. Henderson was one of the founders of the Empire Real Estate Board and founder of the Henderson Realty Company, a pioneer realty company located on Auburn Avenue. A self-educated man, he was made an honorary alumnus of Morehouse College. Long-time supporters of the college, Henderson and his wife contributed a stained-glass window and painting for Morehouse's Danforth Chapel.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Realtist, Civic Worker. A former teacher, she became an associate of the Henderson Realty Company. She was president of the Atlanta Federation of Women's Clubs and president of the Atlanta Metropolitan Council of Negro Women. She was an active church worker at Liberty Baptist, and she devoted time to civic affairs, including the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA, Community Chest, and local and national health organizations.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Porter. Born enslaved in Jackson, Mississippi, Henry entered the Civil War as a servant but soon deserted to serve with Union forces aboard a U.S. cruiser. After the war, Henry worked as a porter for the New York Life Insurance Company in Savannah, managed by J. C. Johnson and Livingston Mims. He stayed with the company when it moved to Atlanta in 1877. In his role as a porter, he handled millions of dollars in bank deposits during his thirty-year career. He also served as personal valet to Mims, who was mayor of Atlanta from 1901 to 1903. Henry was one of the organizers of the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company. He served in the Georgia volunteer infantry and was involved in various civic and community organizations. He was a Mason and he was affiliated with the Colored Teachers Association. He was also a member of the state central committee of the Republican Party. Henry served as president on the board of trustees for the Carrie Steele orphanage, and he was president of Atlanta's Negro Historical Society.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Actor. Born in Savannah, Georgia, Herndon graduated from Atlanta University. She was the first wife of Alonzo Herndon and one of the first African American faculty members at her alma mater. She taught elocution and staged Shakespearean productions with her students. She took the first step in realizing her dream of becoming a professional actor when she made her debut in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1904. She used the stage name "Anne Du Bignon" and recited from Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra. Herndon graduated in 1908 from the School of Dramatic Arts in New York City, furthering her preparation in college teaching and drama production, but she would never become a working actor. Instead, she channeled her natural creativity into teaching and designing "Diamond Hill," the family's two-story, fifteen-room mansion. In 2000, the Herndon home was designated a National Historic Landmark. She died of Addison's disease only three months after the house was completed.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Entrepreneur, Philanthropist. Herndon was the founder of Atlanta Life Insurance Company.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Beautician, Insurance Executive. A native of Milwaukee, Wisconsin, she worked as a hairdresser and manicurist in the Chicago, Illinois, beauty shop belonging to her half-sister. She was the second wife of Alonzo Herndon. He arranged her appointment to the board of the Atlanta Life Insurance Company shortly before his death. She was the first female to serve on the board. Following Alonzo Herndon's death, she was elected Atlanta Life's first female vice president.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Insurance Executive, Philanthropist. Herndon succeeded his father, Alonzo F. Herndon, as president of Atlanta Life Insurance Company. Before moving into the family mansion designed by his mother, Adrienne McNeil Herndon, he lived part of his childhood in the Bumstead Cottage on the campus of Atlanta University. The two-story home had been built by the University's second president, Horace Bumstead. Previously, the Herndons had lived in the boarding house belonging to Francis Norris. Norris Herndon was a graduate of Atlanta University and the business school of Harvard University. As Alonzo Herndon's only heir, he was groomed to manage the family business and fulfill civic and social obligations. In 1905, while still a child, he accompanied his father to the organizing meeting of the Niagara Movement, an early civil rights group. Herndon family biographer Carole Merritt has noted the younger Herndon's struggles with identity and sexuality. He grew up to be a quiet, reclusive man. He managed Atlanta Life with conservative, yet successful strategies, that grew the company into one of the largest African American businesses in the nation. Like his father, he was well regarded for his philanthropy to organizations such as the United Negro College Fund, the NAACP, and the National Urban League.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Jazz Pianist, Arranger, Composer. Heywood, born in Atlanta, was the house pianist at the Village Vanguard in Greenwich Village, New York, in the 1940s. His early musical training and performing experience was with his father, Eddie Heywood Sr., an Atlanta jazz pianist and pit band leader at Bailey's 81 Theater who played for vaudeville acts such as Butterbeans and Susie. Heywood Jr. performed with Wayman Carver in Atlanta and Benny Carter in New York. He formed a sextet which included trumpeter Doc Cheatham and trombonist Vic Dickenson. They performed and recorded with Bing Crosby on records, radio, and film. The group also occasionally backed Billie Holiday. The younger Heywood reached the height of his popularity in the 1940s, but he experienced a partial paralysis of his hands that hampered his performing career. As a composer, he wrote more than forty songs, including "Land of Dreams," "Soft Summer Breeze," and "Canadian Sunset." He was also widely known for his arrangement of Cole Porter's "Begin the Beguine."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: An Atlanta jazz pianist and pit band leader at Bailey's 81 Theater, he played for vaudeville acts such as Butterbeans and Susie. He was the father of jazz pianist Eddie Heywood Jr.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Jazz Pianist, Composer. Born in Atlanta, Hicks and his family moved to Los Angeles, California, when he was still an infant, and later to St. Louis, Missouri. He studied at Lincoln University in Missouri, the Berklee School of Music in Boston, and the Juilliard School in New York. Hicks performed with many jazz greats, including Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, singers Betty Carter and Della Reese, and Woody Herman's big band. During the 1980s and 1990s, he was a highly sought after solo recording artist. He also led his own big band. Two of his most enduring compositions were written as poems. "Naima's Love Song" was written following the birth of his daughter, and "After the Morning" was written after the death of his mother.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Businessman, Civic Leader. Though he never held a political office, Hill was influential in city affairs and an advisor to city leaders, including Atlanta mayors Sam Massell, Andrew Young, Maynard Jackson, and Kasim Reed. He also advised Martin Luther King Jr. and former Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter. Hill became the first African American president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce and the first African American member, and later chair, of the Board of Regents of Georgia's University System. He also served as board chair of the Martin Luther King Jr. Center. A portion of Butler Street was renamed in his honor. Hill was known for his ability to forge alliances between white and African American leaders. Hill earned an MBA in actuarial science from the University of Michigan and went on to become the third president of Atlanta Life Insurance Company. Hill helped launch the Atlanta Inquirer newspaper in the summer of 1960 as a voice of protest against racial discrimination and as an outlet for positive media exposure for the Civil Rights Movement.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician, Fraternal Leader. A graduate of the University of Michigan, Hill taught pharmacy courses at Meharry Medical College while pursuing his medical degree. He was medical director of the Atlanta Life Insurance Company and a member of the board of directors. He was elected president of the National Medical Association in 1936. Hill was president of the Clark College Alumni Association, and he served as grand master of the Georgia York Rite Masons. He married Viola Juanita Miller.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A popular English and journalism instructor, she was chair of the English department at Morris Brown College. She earned her PhD at Indiana University.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Journalist, Civil Rights Leader. Hodges was a sociology professor and department chair at Clark College and later served as dean of Albany State College. He also worked as city editor for the Atlanta Daily World newspaper. In the 1940s, Hodges was chairman of the administrative board of the Atlanta chapter of the NAACP. When ordered by a judge to turn over a list of NAACP members, Hodges would not comply. Hodges married Ruth Beatrice Hall.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She taught art and biology and chaired the art department at Morris Brown College. She earned a master's degree in religious education from Gammon Theological Seminary and a doctorate in education from New York University. She was the first African American woman in Atlanta to own a photography studio. In 1982, Morris Brown named the campus art gallery in her honor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Son of Virgil Wendell Hodges and Ruth Beatrice Hall Hodges. He graduated from Morris Brown College. He was active in the Forward Atlanta campaign in the late 1960s and early 1970s. For a few years, he taught and coached football at Philander Smith College, in Little Rock, Arkansas. He moved to New York where he earned a master's degree in social anthropology from New York University. In New York, he served as deputy commissioner of labor and the executive director of the Martin Luther King Jr. Institute for Nonviolence. Hodges was a member of the board of directors of the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Holsey was a bishop in the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church, later renamed the Christian Methodist Episcopal Church.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Howard was born in Greenville, Georgia. Her father purchased his freedom during slavery and worked hard to achieve literacy. In Atlanta, he started a business as a carriage maker, and she attended the Storrs school. She earned a teaching certificate at Atlanta University. She continued her studies and in 1887 graduated at the head of Spelman Seminary's first high school graduating class. Howard traveled as a missionary to the Congo and spent five years in Africa in charge of a school of 100 students. Recurring bouts of malaria forced her return to the U. S., but she brought with her a young African girl, Flora Zeto Malekebu, to be educated at Spelman. Howard headed the boarding school department at Spelman for twenty-nine years and served as president of the alumnae association. A dormitory at Spelman was named in her memory. The epitaph on her gravestone reads, "An unselfish, useful life."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. Howard was one of the few African American undertakers in 1880s Atlanta. He married Ella Branner.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Born in Summerville, Georgia, she came to Atlanta to attend the Storrs school. She was the first president of the Gate City Free Kindergarten Association and president of the Old Daughters of Bethel. An avid gardener, she filled her yard with a colorful array of flowers and rare plants that she graciously shared with friends and neighbors. She organized the first Atlanta Women's Club for African American women, an affiliate of the National Association of Colored Women.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Educator. Hubert served as director of the School of Religion and professor of church history at Morehouse College. He was acting president of the college from 1937 until 1940. He also served as pastor of Providence Baptist Church. A graduate of Morehouse and Rochester Theological Seminary, Hubert was awarded a doctor of divinity degree by Morehouse for his many achievements. He married Mamie Jones.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Charles Dubois Hubert.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Student. Hubert was the eighteen-year-old nephew of Rev. Charles D. Hubert and a divinity student at Morehouse College. He was accused of insulting a white American woman and attacked at the Crogman Elementary School playground by the woman's husband and six others. One of the men assassinated Hubert with a shot to the back of his head. He was the son of Rev. Gaddus Johnson Hubert, pastor of Wheat Street Baptist, and Pearl M. Parks (d. 1942), principal of Crogman's evening school. During the trial of his attackers, his parents' home was burned down by an unidentified arsonist, and his father's church was bombed with tear gas during a prayer meeting. Hubert's shooter was convicted of voluntary manslaughter and given a sentence of twelve to fifteen years in prison. The six other men were convicted of accessory to murder and received sentences of one to three years. Hubert's murder was one of six recorded lynchings that occurred in Georgia in 1930.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. In 1912, Henry M. Ivey and his brother James E. Ivey founded Ivey Brothers Funeral Home. Both their parents died when the brothers were still children, and they grew up in the Carrie Steele orphanage with their two brothers, R. J. and Nathaniel, and a sister, Estelle. The Ivey Brothers Funeral Home carried the motto, "An institution with a soul." Perhaps due to their upbringing, the Ivey brothers developed a successful business noted for its generosity toward the poor, local churches, and charitable organizations. Henry, originally vice president and also a trained embalmer, succeeded his brother James as company president. His daughter Clara succeeded him as owner of the funeral home.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. In 1912, James E. Ivey and his brother Henry M. Ivey founded Ivey Brothers Funeral Home. James, the first president of the company, graduated from Echols Embalming School and the U.S. Embalming School. The brothers grew up in the Carrie Steele orphanage after both their parents died.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Sister of Henry M. and James E. Ivey. A Spelman nursing school graduate, she worked as a bookkeeper for Ivey Brothers Funeral Home and served as secretary and treasurer.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician. Jackson was a musical prodigy and the son of a musical mother. As a child, he could play virtually any instrument without instruction. He began giving concerts on piano and organ while still in high school. In Atlanta, he performed at the Royal Theater and Bailey's 81 Theater, and he attended Morehouse College and Atlanta University. In 1928, Jackson was appointed head of the music department at Booker T. Washington High School. He served in WWII and performed for the public at war bond rallies. Jackson received multiple citations for raising millions of dollars for U.S. troops. Jackson played for seven U. S. presidents from Franklin Roosevelt to Ronald Reagan. Jackson built his Atlanta home as a replica of Roosevelt's "Little White House" in Warm Springs. Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter designated Jackson as Georgia's official musician. Jackson gained national exposure when his photo appeared in Life Magazine in 1945. He was pictured with a tear-stained face while playing the accordion as the funeral train bearing the body of President Roosevelt left Warm Springs, Georgia. Jackson was also a church musician. He was the organist for St. Paul of the Cross Catholic Church and choir director and organist for First Congregational Church. He married educator Helen B. Jackson.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Graham Washington Jackson.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A professor of French at Spelman College, Jackson earned master's and doctoral degrees at the University of Toulouse in France. She was chair of the department of foreign languages at North Carolina Central University for almost twenty years. In 1933, she married Rev. Maynard Jackson in Toulouse, and the two spent their honeymoon on the French Riviera. She became a widow in 1953. Jackson was the first African American to receive a library card from the main branch of the Atlanta Public Library (APL). In March 1959, Howard Zinn, a history professor at Spelman, and Whitney Young, dean of Atlanta University's school of social work, started a federal lawsuit against APL with two plaintiffs, Jackson and Rev. Otis Moss, a Morehouse theology student. However, the APL board agreed to desegregate without a court battle, and Jackson applied and received a library card. Earl A. Sanders, professor of music at Spelman, received his card at the same time. According to Jackson's daughter Constance, they received threatening phone calls and were harassed by "drive-by incidents" over the next few days. Dobbs was the daughter of John Wesley and Irene Thompson Dobbs. Her eldest son, Maynard Holbrook Jackson, Jr., became Atlanta's first African American mayor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Social Worker, Educator. Simon served as dean of the school of social work at Atlanta University in the 1960s. Under his leadership, the program was accredited by the Council of Social Work Education, the first to be accredited at a historically black college or university. In New York, Jackson was director of the city's Community Action Program, and he founded the city's first adoption agency for children of color. Simon was the first African American executive for the Social Security Administration to be appointed in the Southeast.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Baseball Player. Johnson was a shortstop, third baseman, and outfielder in the Negro Baseball League. He played for the Birmingham Black Barons with Willie Mays, the Indianapolis Clowns with Hank Aaron, the New Orleans Creoles, and the Kansas City Monarchs. After retirement from baseball, he opened and managed a pool hall in Atlanta.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Journalist, Actor, Cinematographer. Jones, an investigative journalist, was also an actor and producer for radio, film, and stage. He preferred to work as a freelancer, and his articles appeared in the Atlanta Daily World, Chicago Defender, Pittsburgh Courier, and Afro-American newspapers. He was well known for his positive depictions of African American life and culture. His newsreel, "Atlanta's Parade of Progress," was shown across the nation in the early 1940s. Admired for his mellow speaking voice, in the 1930s, Jones' dramatic readings were featured on two NBC radio programs, "Welcome Valley," where he was the only African American in a cast of thirty-six, and "Life of Uncle Ned," a portrayal of African American life. Jones also produced and hosted his own popular radio show, "Songs of the Southland," featuring the Swanee River Quartette. His broadcast aired on Atlanta's WGST radio station and included poetry, song, and "homely" philosophy. Richardson earned a reputation as a courageous photojournalist. As a member of the Citizens' Defense Committee, he photographed evidence of brutality and civil rights violations. Among the many Georgia cases Jones investigated were the 1946 Moore's Ford lynchings in Monroe, the killing of Henry Gilbert near LaGrange, and the 1948 death penalty sentence given by an all-white American jury in Ellaville for Rosa Lee Ingram and her teenaged sons, Wallace and Samuel.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A graduate of Atlanta University and Columbia University, in 1920, Jones was appointed the first supervisor of African American elementary schools in Atlanta. In 1934, she was appointed the first female president of the Colored Branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association. In 1935, she became the first female president of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association, an African American organization. She was also well known for her civic and community work, and she was one of the charter members of the Neighborhood Union. An Atlanta public school was named in her honor. She married Alfred Dionysius Jones.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician, Journalist. He was a native of Perry, Georgia, and he graduated from Morehouse College and Howard University Medical School. In Atlanta, he conducted a private practice and directed the health department at Morehouse. He served as president of the Atlanta Medical Association. An avid sportsman, for many years he was sports editor for the Atlanta Independent newspaper.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Caterer. Jordan owned and operated her self-named catering business on Howell Mill Road in an affluent white American area of Atlanta. She originally catered from her home with only a friend to assist her, but by the 1970s, Mary Jordan's Catering Service employed more than thirty staffers, including a bridal consultant. Jordan estimated that nearly ninety-nine percent of her clients were white Americans, and many were third generation customers. Though she hired experienced cooks and servers, Jordan trained all her employees in the art of preparing food her way. In 1972, Jordan received a national Pacesetter award from the national Office of Minority Business Enterprise. In addition to her catering business, Jordan was the proprietor of Lake Jordan, a family recreational area that offered boating, fishing, picnicking, and golf for African Americans. One of her sons, Windsor Jordan, worked in the catering business, first as manager, then as CEO. Another son, Vernon Jordan, was executive director of the National Urban League.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Domestic Servant. Kent was born in Georgia about 1850. He served as the valet of Alexander H. Stephens while Stephens was a U.S. Congressman and when he was governor of Georgia. Stephens had served the Confederacy as vice president during the Civil War. Kent lived with Stephens at his home, Liberty Hall, in Crawfordville, Georgia, and went with him when he traveled to the nation's capital. Stephens died in 1883 and in his will bequeathed $200 to Kent. Kent then worked for Georgia senator Joseph E. Brown until the senator's death in 1894. Brown had been governor of Georgia during the Civil War. Kent found employment as a day laborer until ill health forced his retirement a few years before his death. Kent acquired a considerable amount of property during his lifetime and owned his home on Rhodes Street in Atlanta. At the time of his death, Kent's estate was worth $4,000.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. Following the death of his brother, Martin Luther King Jr., King became co-pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church with his father, Martin Luther King Sr. As a civil rights activist, he had joined his brother in various efforts. During the Birmingham operation, while he was pastor of First Street Baptist Church, his home in Ensley, Alabama, was bombed. He led demonstrations in Louisville, Kentucky, where he pastored Zion Baptist Church. His protests eventually produced an open housing law in Kentucky. In Atlanta, he served on the board of the SCLC. He also worked in the Poor People's Campaign. King drowned in the swimming pool of his Atlanta home. The coroner determined that no foul play was involved in his death.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Realtist. King served as the first steward for the Atlanta Athletic Club and later worked for the University Club. Both were private clubs for white American men. He traveled with Georgia Senator Hoke Smith to Washington D. C. as his messenger. Through Smith's influence, King-who was of mixed African American and American Indian ancestry-was appointed the only American Indian member of the Dawes Commission, which administered the division of tribal lands among American Indians living in the Oklahoma territory. In the summer of 1918, he opened King's Wigwam, a forty-five-acre resort for African Americans that was located in Kennesaw, Georgia. The resort featured cabins, a dance pavilion, tennis courts, and an artificial lake which many church groups used for baptisms. In 1919, King helped organize Mercy Hospital for African Americans in Atlanta, and he served as the hospital's superintendent. King was a trustee of Morris Brown College and a chairman of the board of trustees of Big Bethel AME Church. He married Lincolnia Victoria Turner. King married a second time to Nina Culver.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was the daughter of Bishop Henry McNeal Turner and Eliza Ann Peacher. She was educated at Wilberforce University in Ohio and Berea College in Kentucky. She died two months after the birth of her first child.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a Spelman College graduate. She met King while working in the United States Patent Office in Washington, D. C. In 1922, King founded the real estate firm of Cornelius King & Son.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Son of Cornelius King. After his father's death, he became president of the business. He was affiliated with the NAACP and the Atlanta Civic and Political League. In 1941, the firm built the first modern African American apartment building on Auburn Avenue named "The Wigwam" in honor of his father's American Indian heritage. A red painted tin sculpture of an American Indian which had adorned the porch of the King home was placed atop the building.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. King was pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church for forty-four years. A pioneer civil rights activist, he was involved in the Atlanta Civic and Political League and the NAACP. He led a voting rights march on Atlanta City Hall in 1936 and advocated for equalization of teacher pay. King also served on the boards of Atlanta University and Morehouse College. His epitaph reads, "I love Everyone," and "Still in Business, Just Moved Upstairs." He married Alberta Williams.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was the daughter of Rev. Adam Daniel and Jennie Williams. She started the choir at Ebenezer while her father was pastor and served as organist and music director. She attended Spelman Seminary and later earned a teaching certificate at Hampton Normal Institute. She taught school for a short time before marrying Martin King Sr. who succeeded her father as pastor of Ebenezer. Their son, Martin Luther King Jr., became an internationally recognized civil rights leader. Alberta King was killed by a deranged gunman as she played "The Lord's Prayer" during Sunday worship service at Ebenezer. Her epitaph reads, "Her life shall be filled with music."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Covered Bridge Builder. King, an Alabama native, learned the art of bridge building from his father, Horace King, a highly regarded covered bridge builder and designer. His father was enslaved, but his mother, Francis Goold Thomas, was a free woman of color. After the Civil War, King and his siblings, Marshall Ney, John Thomas, Annie Elizabeth, and George, worked together as the King Brothers Bridge Company. They built bridges and buildings in Georgia and Alabama. Some of Washington King's bridges remain in Georgia today: Watson Mill Bridge in Comer, Georgia; Euharlee Creek Bridge near Cartersville in Bartow County; and Indian Island Bridge in Stone Mountain Park, originally built on the Oconee River in Clarke County. King married Georgia Swift.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a native of Athens, Georgia. She graduated from Atlanta University and taught school in Augusta, Georgia. She served as president of the Georgia Women's Christian Temperance Union. In 1897, she spoke on "Mothers' Meetings" at Atlanta University during the second annual conference on the Social and Physical Condition of Negroes in Cities. She also organized the Sociological Club of Atlanta, which studied the conditions of Atlanta's African American poor and ways to improve their lives.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Beauty Shop Operator. A graduate of Atlanta's Apex Beauty School, Lewis worked as a hair stylist and scalp specialist in Cleveland, Ohio, and Grand Rapids, Michigan. She also served as a national demonstrator for the Persulan Products Company of Detroit, Michigan. She returned to Atlanta in 1954 and became manager of the Bronner Beauty Lounge on Auburn Avenue. Lewis was the sister of Dale and Nathaniel Bronner, well known hair and beauty product suppliers. She married Henderson Lewis who was also associated with Bronner Brothers.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Minister. Lewis served as both the sixth and eighth president of Morris Brown College. He began his teaching career at Payne Institute in Cuthbert, Georgia, before leaving to attend Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut. He completed a bachelor of divinity degree at Yale in 1913 and a master's degree from the University of Chicago in 1914. He taught at Morris Brown beginning in 1915 and served his first term as president from 1920 to 1928. He was ordained as a minister of the AME Church and pastored Trinity Church in Atlanta. Lewis resigned from Morris Brown following the college's financial decline and declaration of bankruptcy. He relocated to Little Rock, Arkansas, where he served as principal of Dunbar High School and president of Shorter College. Moving on to Ohio, he served as dean of Payne Theological Seminary at Wilberforce University. He also continued to be an active pastor, and eventually, he returned to Morris Brown. At the time of his death, Lewis was in the eighth year of his second term as president. A high school in his hometown of Ellaville, Georgia, was named in his honor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Librarian. A native of Los Angeles, California, Lewis graduated from California State College in Los Angeles, and she earned a master's degree in library science from the University of Southern California. Lewis volunteered with Operation Crossroads Africa, and she taught for two years with the U.S. Peace Corps in Yaba, Nigeria. Lewis attended the 1972 Democratic National Convention as a delegate for Shirley Chisholm. Chisholm was the first African American woman to run for the office of U.S. president. In Atlanta, Lewis worked as a librarian at Atlanta University. In 1984, she became the associate director of the Institute for International Affairs and Development at Atlanta University. After the merger of Atlanta University and Clark College, she was appointed director of external affairs in the Office of Research and Sponsored Programs. She married U. S. Congressman John Lewis. She was her husband's chief advisor in his successful campaign for Georgia's 5th District Congressional seat.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. Linder was the son of Reconstruction-era congressman George W. Linder. He graduated from Morris Brown College and worked his way through Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee. He began his practice in his hometown of Dublin, Georgia, but relocated to Atlanta. He served as president of the Atlanta Medical Association and the Georgia Medical Association (GMA), and he started the GMA's first quarterly medical journal. Linder was also a member of the executive board of the National Medical Association. All three associations were professional organizations for African American healthcare practitioners.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Bookkeeper. Lloyd was one of the original performers in "Heaven Bound," a folk drama produced by Big Bethel AME Church since 1930. Over the years, she played the roles of angel, scroll reader, and Saint Cecilia. Lloyd was a member of the Independent Daughters of Bethel and held the position of secretary for that organization for twenty-five years. She was employed as the bookkeeper for Hanley's Bell Street Funeral Home.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Lawyer. Lofton was one of the earliest African American lawyers to practice in Atlanta. Born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, he attended the college preparatory program at Atlanta University. He returned to Tennessee to study law and in 1886, he received his bachelor of arts degree from the law department of Central Tennessee College in Nashville. He began his law practice in Chattanooga but relocated to Atlanta in 1890 and opened an office on Whitehall Street. In 1891, Lofton formed a partnership with J. Robert Davis. Lofton and Davis were the only African American lawyers practicing in Atlanta at that time. Both died young. Davis died of pneumonia in 1894. Lofton contracted tuberculosis and died two years later at the age of thirty-four.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A graduate of Atlanta University in 1883, Luckie moved to Huntsville, Texas, to teach at the newly opened Bishop Ward Normal Institute, the first African American high school in Huntsville. He served as the school's professor of sciences and principal of normal training. He was also a member of the city school board. After four years at Ward, he joined the faculty of Prairie View State Normal and Industrial College where he taught English and history and served as treasurer. At the time of his death, he was assistant principal at Prairie View. A public school in Huntsville was named in his memory.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician, Mortician. Lyons was a graduate of the Atlanta College of Mortuary Science. He was also a popular jazz organist and band leader; he performed in Atlanta and throughout the Southeast. Lyons trained and worked as an embalmer and assistant manager of a funeral home in Detroit, Michigan. In Atlanta, he worked for Sellers Brothers Funeral Home. He died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after he allegedly shot and wounded Valmy Thomas, a catcher for the Atlanta Crackers baseball team. Lyons' funeral was held at Ebenezer Baptist Church, and the service was conducted by his friend, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Members of the Lyons Combo served as active pallbearers. Musicians from throughout the city served as honorary pallbearers. Lyons married Ernestine Sellers.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was the daughter of James H. Sellers, founder of Sellers Brothers Funeral Home. She graduated from Spelman College and attended the New York Academy of Business. She worked as a secretary and bookkeeper for her family's business before rising to the position of manager and later vice president. She was one of the organizers of the Women's Auxiliary of the Georgia Funeral Directors and Practitioners Association. Sellers was also an adult leader and board member of the Atlanta Girl Scouts. In 1950, she led a scout group to the regional council meeting in Miami, Florida, and on a tour of Cuba.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Missionary. When she was still a young girl, Flora Zeto was brought from Africa to Atlanta by Spelman graduate and missionary Clara A. Howard. In 1915, Zeto became the first student from the Congo to graduate from Spelman. She married Daniel Sharpe Malekebu, another child brought from Africa by Spelman missionary Emma Delany. Malekebu received his medical degree from Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee. Flora and Daniel returned to Africa to do missionary work but frequently visited the United States. Spelman's Gordon-Zeto Center for Global Education was named in her honor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner. Ramsey owned and operated a beauty shop on Auburn Avenue. In St. Louis, she worked with African American beauty expert and millionaire business woman Annie M. Malone of the Poro Beauty College. When Martin moved to Atlanta, she founded the Poro School of Beauty Culture with financing from Annie Malone. Ramsey was an astute business person; she organized the Atlanta Beauty Culturists League and the Georgia State Beauty Culturists League for licensed beauticians. Community involvement was key to Martin's process-some beauty shops in the league offered voter registration; others gave free services for children and the elderly. Martin served as president of the Georgia State Beauty Culturists League for twenty-two years.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Insurance Executive. A native of Atlanta, Martin attended Atlanta University. He began his career with the Atlanta Life Insurance Company in 1912 and stayed with the company for fifty-seven years. Martin was a member of the Hughes Spalding Pavilion Advisory Committee, vice chairman of the board of the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home, and a member of the board of directors of the national NAACP. He eventually served Atlanta Life as chief executive officer and in the roles of first vice president and secretary. At the annual stockholders' meeting held just a few months before his death, Martin was presented with a gold Lucien Piccard watch for distinguished service to Atlanta Life. He married Helen White, who at one time worked as a secretary for the Atlanta Life Insurance Company. Like her brother, civil rights leader and NAACP executive director Walter White, she was a native of Atlanta and attended Atlanta University.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Sexton. "Brother" Matthews was the sexton of Big Bethel AME Church for more than fifty years. Matthews originated the role of St. Peter in 1930 in the church's annual musical drama, "Heaven Bound." Before becoming sexton at Big Bethel, Matthews worked as a janitor at the First Methodist Church. He had also worked for a number of years in the hotel industry. Matthews served in the Georgia militia as quartermaster in the Governor's Volunteers. The year before his death, he participated in the Georgia exhibit at Chicago's second world's fair. Matthews was struck by a hit and run driver while on his way to church at Big Bethel. A month later, he died as a result of his injuries. He was ninety-three years old. He was a class leader at Big Bethel; he led the largest class in the church and typically led the classes in fundraising.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Model, Fashion Designer. A former Ebony Fashion Fair model, Mattison had just embarked on a career in fashion design when he drowned in an accident off the coast of Fire Island in New York. As a teenager, Mattison was a talented scholar, musician, and artist. He organized his own summer theater workshop for the neighborhood children, "The Little Theater of the Stars." The workshop ended with a performance-Mattison not only prepared the young actors, he also painted the backgrounds, managed the sound system, and designed the costumes. Mattison's image appeared in most major magazines and newspapers and on billboards throughout the U.S. He was a graduate of Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, and he studied music at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts in Philadelphia. Lincoln University established a music and art scholarship in his memory. His burial crypt bears his portrait.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner. Previously, she had owned and operated the Mackie Bee Hotel. In 1926, McBride opened the fifty-room Hotel McKay on Auburn Avenue. It was located on the second and third floors of the Citizen Trust Company Bank building. The McKay was McBride's second hotel in Atlanta. The new hotel catered to businessmen and traveling salesmen by offering private conference facilities. For young married couples, the McKay provided "handsomely furnished suites.'' McBride also operated a taxi service, and she owned a row of shotgun rental houses located on Boulevard.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Nurse. For thirty-five years, McFarlin worked as a public health nurse in various Atlanta clinics that served African Americans. She also made house calls and visited housing projects and schools. McFarlin was noted for her special rapport with young children. A native Atlantan, she attended Booker T. Washington High School and graduated from Grady Memorial Hospital School of Nursing. She also worked as a private duty nurse and for the federal Works Progress Administration during the Great Depression. During WWII, she was an American Red Cross nurse. McFarlin volunteered with Matrons Rendering Service (MRS), a women's club that assisted African Americans in need.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. McLendon was a native of Washington, Georgia, and a graduate of Meharry Medical College, in Nashville, Tennessee. In 1946, he opened the McLendon Medical Clinic in Atlanta for African Americans. By the time the hospital closed in 1981, more than fifty African American and four hundred white American doctors had trained at McLendon. The hospital offered services in surgery, dental care, plastic surgery, obstetrics, and pediatrics. While serving as president of the Atlanta Medical Association (AMA), McLendon wired Martin Luther King Jr. to offer doctors and medical aid to victims of police brutality in Selma, Alabama. McLendon was a life member of the NAACP, and he was referred to by Jet magazine as a "militant medic." He joined AMA doctors in demonstrations for equal pay for African Americans, and he was arrested along with other doctors attending a medical conference at Atlanta's Biltmore Hotel when they attempted to eat lunch at the hotel's segregated cafeteria. McLendon received the first gold medallion awarded by the Georgia State Medical Association. He was also a real estate investor and developed the Crestwood Forest subdivision. McLendon married Bennie Bell.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a graduate of Fisk University, in Nashville, Tennessee, and taught for a short time at the high school level and at Fisk. Her husband referred to her as the "brain power" behind the medical facility, and she served as secretary of the McLendon Hospital for thirty-five years. At various times, she served as president for the Women's Auxiliary of the Atlanta Medical Association, the Georgia State Medical Association, and the National Medical Association. The McLendon family operated a variety of businesses, including a grocery store, drugstore, mortuary, and real estate office. They were the founders and developers of the Royal Oaks Manor community. She was the first president and co-founder of the Atlanta Links chapter and national vice president of The Links, Inc. She was also affiliated with the YWCA, Gate City Day Nursery, and League of Women's Voters. She was a lifetime member of the NAACP. Along with Dorothy Alexander, she led the protest to desegregate the annual Atlanta performances of the Metropolitan Opera at the Fox Theater.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Librarian. McPheeters was the first professionally trained African American librarian to work in the Atlanta Public Library system. She earned a bachelor's degree in library science from Hampton Institute in Virginia and a master's degree in library science from Columbia University in New York. McPheeters worked as a public librarian in Greenville, South Carolina, before being hired in 1934 as assistant librarian at the Auburn Branch of the Atlanta Public Library. Two years later, she was promoted to branch manager. In 1949, she moved to the West Hunter Branch as manager. McPheeters achieved another "first" in 1966 when she became the first African American reference librarian at Georgia State University. The West Hunter Branch Library was renamed in her honor as the Washington Park/ Annie L. McPheeters Branch Library. McPheeters collected materials on African American history and culture to develop the collection that formed the basis of the Auburn Avenue Research Library (AARL). The Cary/McPheeters Gallery at AARL was established in memory of McPheeters and the first African American librarian of the Auburn Avenue branch, Alice Dugged Cary. AARL conducts the Annie L. McPheeters Lecture Series and School Project in her memory.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Architect. Miller was a member of the American Institute of Architects. He earned his degree in architecture from New York University and taught architecture at Tuskegee University. In Atlanta, Miller's architectural firm provided practical experience for African American student architects. He married Nina King.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Realtist. She was the first woman to be elected treasurer of the Empire Real Estate Board. She was the daughter of Cornelius and Nina Culver King and followed her father into the real estate business.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner, Banker, Educator. Milton was president of Citizens Trust Bank and a partner in the Yates and Milton drugstore chain. He graduated from Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, with his bachelor's and master's degrees. John Hope, the first African American president of Morehouse College in Atlanta, and a graduate of Brown, asked Milton to join the teaching staff at Morehouse. With his partners, Clayton Yates and Jesse B. Blayton, Milton was involved in a number of other business ventures, including the Top Hat club, Brown Boy Bottling Company, and Southeastern Fidelity Fire Insurance Company. Milton also served on the board of the South-View Cemetery Association. Milton continued to teach at Morehouse while working at Citizens Trust.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Dancer. A native Atlantan, Mitchell was the owner of Norman's Academy of Fine Arts, established in 1973. It was the first interdisciplinary multicultural arts program for children and adults in southwest Atlanta. Classes included ballet, French, tap, jazz, piano, organ, guitar, drama, modeling, and charms and social graces. The Academy also featured fitness classes and a music and dance library. Mitchell graduated from Morris Brown College and continued her education at Emory and Atlanta universities. She taught biology at Morris Brown and served on the National Science Foundation in Washington, D. C. As part of its community arts program, the Academy offered scholarships to promising young dancers. Mitchell's daughter, Djana Bell-Rawlings, continued to operate the academy after her mother's death.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Laborer, Churchman. Called "Father Montgomery," he was one of the founders of Big Bethel AME Church and served on the original board of trustees. He secured the land for the church's first building from Lemuel P. Grant, who also donated land to the city for Atlanta's Grant Park. Montgomery was born enslaved in Buck Creek, Jackson County, Georgia, in 1808. He died in Atlanta at the Colored Old Folks Home, which he had helped raise funds to build. While on a fundraising trip to Washington, D. C., Montgomery met and shook hands with President William McKinley. During slavery, his brother Ransom Montgomery gained local notoriety when he prevented a railroad bridge from being destroyed by fire, saving the lives of more than one hundred train passengers. Father Montgomery's memories of Atlanta's early history were recorded in E. R. Carter's 1894 history of African American life in Atlanta, "The Black Side."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician, Educator. Montgomery was a pianist and band leader in 1920s Atlanta. He toured with his own orchestra in the 1930s and 1940s. Montgomery performed with a variety of talented musicians, including singer Ella Fitzgerald, drummer Chick Webb, and fellow Atlantan, jazz flutist Wayman Carver. Two of his well-known songs had local associations: "Atlanta Lowdown" and "Auburn Avenue Stomp." Montgomery was one of the organizers of Local 462 of the American Federation of Musicians and served as the first president. He worked as a promoter and formed the Southeastern Artists Bureau to bring African American musicians and entertainers to Atlanta. In the early 1950s, he wrote a column for the Atlanta Journal/Constitution, "Weekly Roundup of News," focused on current events about African Americans. Montgomery taught at Booker T. Washington High and David T. Howard schools and worked for the Atlanta Board of Education for more than forty years. He married Callie Mae Washburn.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. She earned a bachelor's degree from Morris Brown College and a master's degree from Atlanta University. She served as a teacher and later principal for the private Oglethorpe Elementary School (also called Laboratory Elementary School) on the campus of Atlanta University.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. Nash received his medical degree in 1910 from Meharry Medical College, in Nashville, Tennessee, and he opened his office on Auburn Avenue the same year. He served as a 1st lieutenant in the U.S. Army Medical Corps in World War I and was later promoted to Captain. An active volunteer in the community, Nash was staff physician to the children of the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home. One of the orphanage's dormitory cottages is named for him. The Atlanta Medical Association, comprised of African American healthcare professionals, established an award in his honor. He was recognized as "physician of the year'' by two other African American medical organizations-the Georgia Medical Association (in 1965) and National Medical Association (in 1963). Nash served as the general secretary of the Georgia State Medical Association.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Pharmacist, Educator. Neal was a graduate of Morehouse College, and he also earned degrees from Atlanta University and Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee. He worked part time as a pharmacist at the Amos Drugstore and at the Yates and Milton drugstore. Neal taught chemistry at Booker T. Washington High School, Spelman and Morehouse colleges, and Atlanta University. He also served as a director of Citizens Trust Bank. Neal was a grand master of the Prince Hall Masons for almost thirty years. He was also well known in international Masonic circles. Liberian President W. S. V. Tubman anointed Neal a Knight Commander of the Liberian Humane Order of African Redemption and also designated him an honorary African chief.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician. A native of Louisiana, he came from a musical family; his father, Versie Nelson, played upright bass and harmonica. He grew up playing zydeco, Cajun, and blues with his father at neighborhood barbecues and fish fries. Nelson was a traditional "Chicago-style" blues harp player and singer. Nelson spent his childhood summers in Chicago where he later met and performed with Muddy Waters who gave him the nickname "Chicago Bob." He also performed with Howlin' Wolf, Earl Hooker, Buddy Guy, and Junior Wells. Nelson toured with John Lee Hooker's Coast to Coast Blues Band for several years. In 2009, the Music Maker Relief Foundation recorded Nelson singing "Tell Me Mama."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Contractor, Civic Leader. Norwood had no formal education, but he used his skills as a brick mason to open the Norwood Construction Company. Norwood was active in the Thomasville community where he lived and in the Bible Way Church. He was an NAACP member and voter registration volunteer. He married Darthula Norwood. In the 1950s, Norwood sold a portion of his land in Thomasville to be used to build houses for African Americans. The Norwood Manor subdivision was built through a cooperative effort involving the Atlanta Urban League, the Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association, and the Roy D. Warren Company. Following the death of his first wife, he married Esther Frances Norwood.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was an active church worker and respected missionary leader.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Oliver was pastor of Warren Memorial Methodist Church from 1906 until his death. He was the son-in-law of the church's first pastor, John Crolley. During his tenure, he increased Warren Memorial's membership to approximately 1,400 congregants and moved the church to the corner of Greensferry and Mildred streets. Oliver had served as presiding elder in the Methodist Episcopal Church from 1901 until 1906. He married Georgia H. Crolley.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She organized the women's missionary society at Warren and presided as the society's first president. They established a Sunday school as part of the Rockdale Park mission in Atlanta. The Rockdale Park mission was the genesis of the Georgia Oliver Memorial United Methodist Church.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. O'Neal was the founder of the National Divine Spiritual Church and served as overseer for thirty-four years. In recognition of Bishop O'Neal's religious and civic leadership, Atlanta Mayor Maynard Jackson proclaimed December 10, 1978, as "Hiram O'Neal Day." His wife, Pauline Ealy, succeeded him as spiritual leader.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She succeeded her husband, Bishop Hiram O'Neal II, as spiritual leader of the National Divine Spiritual Church. Both O'Neal and his wife received spiritual training at the Progressive Spiritual School of John R. Drummond.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Grandfather and namesake of Bishop Hiram O'Neal II. He was a highly-regarded building contractor. Although unable to read and write, he was considered an astute businessman.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Pace founded one of the first orphanages for African American children in Georgia. Born enslaved in Athens, Georgia, she moved with her family to Atlanta after the end of the Civil War. Along with help from her brothers Lewis and Albert Watts, she started a Sunday School in their neighborhood that grew into Reed Street Baptist Church (today, Paradise Missionary Baptist Church). Pace graduated from Atlanta University with a teaching certificate and started her first teaching assignment in Covington, Georgia. She had expected to remain in Covington only two years, but in 1890 she resigned her teaching position and chartered the Covington Colored Orphans Home. The home was later renamed the Reed Home and School for Colored Children, in honor of Mrs. A. C. Reed, a major benefactor. She married a local blacksmith, James F. Pace, who provided furnishings for the home, and she traveled extensively to raise funds for the orphans. Her brother Lewis, a Pullman Porter, helped her financially, and the students of Wellesley College in Massachusetts were regular contributors to her cause. Pace also had another talent. She was known locally as a "dream reader," and Covington residents would consult her for dream interpretations before they played the numbers in the neighborhood lottery. The orphanage and school operated until the 1930s. Pace was badly burned when she suffered a fainting spell and fell into the flames of an open fireplace. She died a few days later.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Parker was the first pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church which he and seven others founded in 1886. The church congregation remained small under Parker's leadership and never grew to more than a few members. Parker served Ebenezer at its Airline Street location until 1894 when Adam Daniel Williams succeeded him as pastor.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Jazz Pianist, Composer. Pearson performed with many widely-recognized jazz artists, such as trumpeter Donald Byrd and vocalist Nancy Wilson. In the 1960s, he was a key influence at Blue Note records where he recorded and worked as a producer. For more than ten years, he led his own group, the Duke Pearson Band, featuring players like Chick Corea and Pepper Adams. Pearson recorded seventeen albums, including "The Right Touch" regarded by some as his crowning achievement. Pearson's uncle nicknamed him "Duke," in honor of Duke Ellington.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. Penn practiced medicine in Atlanta for twenty-five years and helped organize the Mercy and Fair Haven medical facilities.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Gospel Singer, Music Educator. Perry and her brother William Guest were cousins of singer Gladys Knight and original members of the singing group, the Pips. Perry was the Atlanta chapter representative of the Gospel Music Workshop of America, and she served on the Fulton County Arts Council. Gladys Knight sang "Blessed Assurance" at Perry's funeral service.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Perry, an Atlanta native, graduated from Atlanta University in 1890. She began her career at the Houston Street School as an assistant teacher then later taught at the Carrie Steele Orphans Home.
