In 1898, she presented a paper on the life of Carrie Steele and the orphanage at the Atlanta University conference on Some Efforts of Negroes for Their Own Social Betterment.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Builder, Contractor. Pharrow was one of the most successful African American contractors in the nation and a self-taught civil and mechanical engineer. He began his contracting business in Birmingham, Alabama. In Atlanta, his work included Flipper Hall at Morris Brown College, Sale Hall at the Atlanta Baptist College (later Morehouse), the First Congregational Church, and the Odd Fellows Building. In 1914, he built the Wage Earner's Bank in Savannah, which later became the site of the Ralph Mark Gilbert Civil Rights Museum. Pharrow was a director of the Atlanta State Savings Bank and a stockholder in several African American corporations. He was also a fraternal leader and held memberships in the Masons, Odd Fellows, Knights of Pythias, and Elks. He was a generous contributor to educational and charitable organizations, and he served on the board of trustees of Morris Brown. He served in various roles as a member of Big Bethel AME Church.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Baseball Player. "Dick" Phillips, a left-hander, played football and baseball at Booker T. Washington High School. While attending Morris Brown College, he was unanimously voted the most outstanding pitcher of the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference. Phillips played in the Georgia Amateur Baseball League with the Atlanta All-Stars and the Atlanta Panthers before signing with the Kansas City Monarchs. Some of Phillips' notable teammates with the Kansas City Monarchs included Satchel Paige, Cool Papa Bell, and Jackie Robinson.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.full_name: Clara C. Thomas Maxwell Cater Pitts
people.biography: Educator. Pitts served as superintendent of the Carrie Steele Orphans Home. During her administration, she updated the operations of the home and relocated it to a new facility on Roy Street in southwest Atlanta. She also secured funding for the home through the Atlanta Community Chest (later part of the United Way). To reflect her years of dedication and service, in 1950 the name of the home was changed to the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home. An Atlanta public school was named in her honor. Her daughter Mae Maxwell Yates succeeded her as director of the home. Pitts married three times: to Rev. Leigh B. Maxwell, to Charles C. Cater, and to Howard Pitts.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A native of Griffin, Georgia, and a third-generation barber, Howard Pitts came to Atlanta as a young man. He worked for fifty years at the Herndon barbershop downtown and served as treasurer of Herndon Barbers, Inc.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
people.spouse: Clara C. Thomas Maxwell Cater Pitts

people.biography: Business Owner, Postmaster. Price, a graduate of the business department of Clark College, operated a general store at the intersection of Jonesboro and McDonough roads. In 1889, Price was appointed the postmaster for the South Atlanta substation, a branch of the U. S. Post Office that he operated inside his store. He was the first and only African American postmaster in Atlanta at that time. The appointment of African American postmasters across Georgia and the South had resulted in numerous cases of bitter opposition and sometimes violence on the part of white Americans. Price's store was located in the predominantly African American community of Brownsville near Clark College's campus, and his initial appointment apparently did not cause much, if any, controversy. The Price family lived above the store until they moved into the new home that Price built on Gammon Avenue in South Atlanta. Price was serving as postmaster for South Atlanta in September 1906 when white Americans rioted in the streets of Atlanta attacking and killing African American citizens. Price was arrested and charged with supplying weapons to African American men to defend themselves from the white American rioters. If he had been found guilty, he would have lost his position as postmaster. The case against Price was dismissed, but he chose to remain in jail for several days for his own safety. An Atlanta school was named in his memory. Price married Minnie Wright.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a graduate of Atlanta University. She was actively involved in missionary endeavors and women's club work. In 1897, she spoke on the topic of "Friendly Visiting" at Atlanta University during the second annual conference on the Social and Physical Condition of Negroes in Cities. She encouraged women to ignore social class and make home visits to those less fortunate as a means of bringing encouragement to the poor and sick.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Proctor was the first African American pastor of First Congregational Church. Organized in 1867, the church held services in Storrs Chapel which was located on the corner of Calhoun and Houston Streets. Initially, the congregation was racially integrated, but by 1877, the church was categorized in the Atlanta Constitution as "colored." Proctor began his ministry at the church in 1894. He was a graduate of Fisk University and Yale Divinity School. Under his leadership, the church began to emphasize neighborhood outreach and community service. The congregation established a lending library, a kindergarten, job training, an employment bureau, classes for the blind, a home for young working women, a gymnasium, and a public water fountain. Proctor organized Atlanta's first "Colored Music Festival." The festival series featured artists like Harry Burleigh, an African American classical composer and baritone soloist. When the First Congregational church laid the cornerstone for a new building in 1908, Booker T. Washington was the featured speaker on the program; George Washington Carver spoke during the building dedication services in 1909. The First Congregational Church is a Georgia Historical Marker site and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Cashier. Redding was the first African American teller and cashier at the white-owned Merchants Bank. He was hired to serve African American customers. As a young boy, Redding began working in the office of Judge George Hillyer, and he eventually gained a legal education by "reading law" with the Judge. In 1870, Redding was elected as an officer for Monroe County for the Macon and Western Railroad, and he served as a delegate to the Democratic State Convention from Monroe. "Colonel" Redding, as he was called, was one of the organizers and president of the Atlanta Loan and Trust company, a real estate investment firm. In 1895, Redding opened the European Hotel to provide accommodations for African Americans traveling to Atlanta for the Cotton States and International Exposition. A commemorative bas relief sculpture located on Auburn Avenue near Hilliard Street pays tribute to his life and contributions to the community. He married Ellen S. Griffin.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A native of Wilkes County, Georgia, she attended the Storrs School in Atlanta. She worked as a teacher for several years before her marriage.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Baseball Player, Educator. Reeves was an "All American" athlete in football and basketball at Clark College. He played in the Negro Baseball League with the Atlanta Black Crackers, the Indianapolis ABCs, and the Chicago American Giants. After his baseball career ended, he taught school in Georgia and Florida for forty years. He was voted "Teacher of the Year" at Sandersville High School in Washington County, Georgia.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Musician. Red McAllister, as he was known professionally, was a band leader and saxophonist. He was also sometimes known as McAllister Evans. He toured with his jazz orchestra throughout the Southeast. In Atlanta, they performed at venues like the Top Hat club. When the Top Hat closed in 1949, Riggins' mother, business woman Carrie Cunningham, bought the building and opened the Royal Peacock night club. The club provided Riggins with a regular place to perform without touring, and he also worked to book other performers for the club. Riggins is credited with composing at least one song, "Peacock Blues," with Henry Glover. Riggins also owned rental property and operated a cab company. Riggins married Rudean H. Riggins.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A native of South Carolina, she graduated from Spelman College and taught in the Atlanta Public Schools for twenty-four years. She volunteered with the Dekalb Medical Center and the American Red Cross.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Civil Rights Leader. A Spelman College graduate, Robinson grew up in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood. While still a teen, she became active in the Civil Rights Movement. She became the first and only woman to serve as executive secretary of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). She organized SNCC chapters and participated in sit-ins and the Freedom Rides. After a South Carolina "jail, no bail" student protest, Robinson and several others served a thirty-day jail sentence, including time on the chain gang. In Mississippi, she suffered a forty-five-day jail term in the Parchman Penitentiary. Her health began to deteriorate, and she was diagnosed with terminal cancer. She died at age twenty-five. Robinson's epitaph reads, "If you think free, you are free."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. The Rush Memorial Congregational Church in Atlanta was named in memory of John Rush. Rush attended Gammon Theological Seminary and served as pastor of Loyd Street Methodist Episcopal Church, later renamed Central Avenue Methodist Episcopal Church (today, Central United Methodist Church). Rush led a group of Central Avenue members to form "The People's Church." Following Rush's death, the congregation voted unanimously to enter the Congregational denomination and changed the name of the church to Rush Memorial. During the Civil Rights Movement, the church served as a meeting place for student activists.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Entrepreneur, Civic Leader, Philanthropist. Russell was born in Atlanta during the Great Depression. His family, like many others, struggled financially, but Russell was industrious. He began shining shoes and selling Coca Colas while still a child, and by age sixteen, he had managed to save $125 to purchase his first piece of property. The rental income financed Russell's college education. He earned a degree in construction from Tuskegee University, but he learned how to run a business from his father. H.J. Russell and Company would eventually help build a considerable portion of Atlanta's skyline. Russell also branched out into other fields-hotels, restaurants, and media. Russell was the first African American member on the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, and the second African American president of the Chamber; the first African American president was his close friend Jesse Hill. Russell was friends with many local and national business and political leaders, including Martin Luther King Jr. During the height of the Civil Rights Movement, Russell financed bail bonds for jailed activists, and he was a major donor to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Russell served as a board member for a number of national corporations and organizations, such as the U. S. Chamber of Commerce, Wachovia Bank, Citizens Trust Bank, and Georgia Power Company. He married Otelia Hackney. Later, he married Sylvia Anderson, former president of AT&T Georgia.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a school teacher. She was a member of the Salvation Army board of directors and a member of the Atlanta chapter of Girl Friends Inc., a community service organization. The Russells funded an endowed chair in entrepreneurship at Clark Atlanta University's School of Business Administration.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Shoemaker, Entrepreneur. Schell arrived in Atlanta in 1876 with a total savings of $3.75. That first night in Atlanta, he had no place to sleep, but he soon found work with A. J. Delbridge, an African American shoemaker. After several more years of working and saving his earnings, Schell opened his own shoe shop. Later, he purchased additional properties to start more businesses, and he also rented space to other business owners. Schell owned dry goods stores, barber shops, and a public hall, Schell's Opera House. The opera house offered a full theater with a stage and was a popular site for political meetings. Schell was one of the founders and the treasurer of the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company. He was also a stockholder in the South-View Cemetery Association. When his home on Auburn Avenue was completed in 1897, it was considered by some to be the finest house owned by any African American in Georgia.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. Sellers attended Tuskegee Institute and South Carolina State College. He worked for the Atlanta Life Insurance Company before going into the mortuary business. His brother Samuel Garrett Sellers attended mortuary school and joined him in business to form Sellers Brothers Funeral Home.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: He attended mortuary school and joined his brother James Horace Sellers in business to form Sellers Brothers Funeral Home. S. G. Sellers served as vice president of the Georgia State Association of Funeral Directors and Embalmers. He was also a district chairman of the Boy Scouts.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: A brother of James Horace Sellers and Samuel Garrett Sellers, he worked in the family business, Sellers Brothers Funeral Home. He was the last surviving brother of the original Sellers brothers.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: He was the son of James H. Sellers. He worked as a funeral director at Sellers Brothers. He was a member of the Atlanta Senior Golf Association and was president and treasurer of Pine Acres Town and Country Club. He served on the board of directors of the Lincoln Country Club.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner. Shaw was an entrepreneur and the secretary of Georgia's Central Republican Committee.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A Spelman graduate, Shelton was an art teacher in the Atlanta Public Schools for fifty years. She was the maternal grandmother of filmmaker Shelton "Spike" Lee. Having saved money from her social security checks for her grandchildren's education, she provided the financial support for Lee to attend Morehouse College. She continued to support her grandson through his graduate studies at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts and provided the seed money for his first feature film, She's Gotta Have It. Spike Lee credits his grandmother with being his inspiration and for making his film and teaching career possible. She married postal worker Richard Jackson Shelton.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Zimmie Reva Shelton.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Shivery was the head of the English department at Booker T. Washington High School, and she authored the school song. She earned her master's degree at Atlanta University. Shivery was a contributing writer for the Atlanta Daily World and an officer for the National Council for Negro Women. She helped establish Atlanta's Neighborhood Union and served as its executive secretary and historian. She served as president of the Atlanta Metropolitan Council of Negro Women and on the board of the Colored Branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Boxer. "Cowboy Kid" began his boxing career at the Ivy Street Garage in Atlanta. In 1928, he defeated Tiger Taylor to become the "Colored Lightweight Champion of the South." He later fought to a draw for the middleweight crown against title holder Sam McVey. The fight proved to be one of his most famous. Simmons died at Grady Hospital from a knife wound to the chest. The fatal injury was inflicted during an altercation between Simmons and William "Bootleg Red" Long.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Sculptor, Painter, Printmaker, Musician, Songwriter. Simon earned her undergraduate degree, summa cum laude, from Atlanta University. At Spelman College, she studied with sculptor Alice Dunbar and painter Hale Woodruff. Simon was the first African American to graduate from the Atlanta College of Art in 1967. Simon was a founding member and officer of the National Conference of Negro Artists. In 1973, Atlanta Mayor Sam Massell appointed her to the Civic Design Commission. She married Edward Lloyd Simon.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Insurance Executive. Starting as a salesman in 1934, Simon moved up through the company ranks to become senior vice president and general auditor for Atlanta Life Insurance Company. He served as president of the National Insurance Association which recognized him with a distinguished service award. After retirement, he was elected chair of the board of directors of Atlanta Life. He also served as chairman of the board of Southern Aid/Life of Virginia, a subsidiary of Atlanta Life. Simon was regarded as a pioneer in interracial cooperation and was an active member of the Kiwanis Club and the Conference of Christians and Jews.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Simon was a highly-regarded alumna and physical education instructor at Spelman College. She graduated from Spelman in 1935 with a degree in biology. She had no formal training in physical education instruction when she was hired in 1943, but she earned a master's degree in physical education in 1960 from the University of Colorado. Due to her influence and support, the physical education department was established at Spelman, and the college's first fitness and recreation center was built in 1950.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Spivey, a teacher in the Atlanta Public Schools, was the last surviving woman of the thirty-three women who graduated from Morehouse College between 1929 and 1933. Spivey was the second woman in her family to be educated at Morehouse; her mother attended classes there in the early 1900s. Spivey graduated in 1933 at age nineteen.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Police Officer, Postal Worker. In 1948, through the efforts of local civil rights activists, Strickland and seven other men desegregated the Atlanta Police Department. In those early years, the eight men used the Butler Street YMCA as their precinct. They were not allowed to wear their uniforms to and from work, and they only patrolled African American sections of the city, on foot. They were not allowed to drive squad cars or arrest white Americans. A native Atlantan, Strickland had attended Morehouse College before serving in the Army during WWII. In 1961, he left the Atlanta force but later helped integrate the Decatur Police Department. Strickland then moved to New York where he worked the next twenty-two years for the U. S. Postal Service (USPS) in Manhattan. Strickland received the Atlanta NAACP Honor Award and the USPS Outstanding Service Award.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Banker, Financial Consultant. Sutton began his career as a bookkeeper for Citizens Trust Bank and rose to the position of executive vice president. He helped many African Americans buy their first homes. Sutton founded a financial consulting business, R. O. Sutton and Associates. He also served as vice president of finance for Paschal's Concession, Inc. at the Atlanta airport. Sutton was a board member of many business and community organizations, including the Atlanta Life Insurance Company, the Butler Street YMCA, and the George Washington Carver Boys and Girls Club.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Restaurant Owner. When Sutton first arrived in Atlanta from Washington, Georgia, she could neither read nor write, but she learned the alphabet by using the Atlanta Weekly Constitution newspaper. She continued to improve her literacy skills as she gained knowledge and experience in business. "Ma" Sutton owned and operated her restaurant on Auburn Avenue for more than thirty years. The name "Ma" was given to her by WWI soldiers who frequented her establishment. At her nationally famous restaurant, Sutton took great pride in serving large portions of good food, and she cultivated a comfortable, yet "classy," atmosphere. "Ma Sutton's" was praised as one of the most outstanding African American restaurants in the South.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Civil Rights Leader. Taylor was a high school science and math teacher in the Atlanta Public Schools. He served as president of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association. He and the Atlanta NAACP sued the board of education to grant equal pay for African American teachers. NAACP lawyer Constance Baker Motley represented the plaintiffs. Motley was later appointed a federal judge in New York. In 1948, a federal court ordered Georgia public schools to equalize teacher pay. Taylor was fired from the Atlanta Public Schools, allegedly not for his role in the lawsuit but for being absent without leave while attending his graduate school reunion. He appealed to the school board and his firing was overturned; however, he was reassigned to an elementary school, and he resigned shortly afterwards. Taylor worked as a conciliations supervisor for the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for seventeen years. He was also a real estate broker and property manager.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Lawyer. An alumnus of Morehouse College, Thomas graduated from the University of Michigan Law School in 1947. With only a few years of experience, in 1953, he served as lead counsel for the plaintiffs in Holmes v. Atlanta, the first desegregation lawsuit to be tried in the city. A group of young African American men were denied the right to play at the Bobby Jones Golf Course, a city-owned course. The case eventually reached the U. S. Supreme Court and resulted in the desegregation of all municipal golf courses in Atlanta. Thomas was a founding member of the Gate City Bar Association and served as its third president. He became a specialist in real estate and probate law. He served as general counsel for Citizens Trust Bank, Atlanta Life Insurance Company, and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan. He was a member of the NAACP and the Urban League.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: U.S. Deputy Marshal, Business Owner, Masonic Leader.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Tillman was highly regarded as a classroom teacher and administrator. He was widely published as a scholarly writer and in great demand as a national speaker and consultant. Tillman graduated from Morehouse College and received master's and doctoral degrees from the University of Wisconsin. He held various positions at Morehouse and Atlanta University, including professor of English and chairman of the English department at both schools. Tillman also served as dean of the school of arts and sciences at Atlanta University. Earlier on the same day that he died, the trustees of Atlanta University held an award ceremony to recognize his twenty-five years of service to the university. His funeral was held in the Dean Sage Auditorium on the campus of Atlanta University.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Executive. Toomer worked for Atlanta Life Insurance Company for almost forty years. A graduate of Atlanta University, he worked his way through school as a bellhop at the Piedmont hotel during the school year and as a Pullman Porter during his summer breaks. Before joining Atlanta Life as a traveling auditor, Toomer worked as an embalmer for funeral homes in North Carolina and Georgia. During his career at Atlanta Life, he was promoted to chief auditor and ultimately to third vice-president. He also served on the board of directors. He was affiliated with the United Negro College Fund and the YMCA. He served as president of the Lincoln Country Club. An Atlanta public school was named in his honor. He married Juanita Paschal.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Journalist. A native of Columbus, Georgia, she began her teaching career at an elementary school in Columbus. She also taught English at Spelman and Morehouse colleges, and she was a reporter for the Atlanta Daily World.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Author, Civil Rights Activist. Towns was one of the first African Americans to join the faculty of Atlanta University. He taught in the English department and coached the debate team. He earned degrees from Atlanta and Harvard universities. His poems and essays were printed in national publications. He also wrote a play, "The Sharecropper." Towns participated in the organizing meeting of the Niagara Movement in 1905, and he was active with the NAACP and African American voter registration. An Atlanta public school was named in his honor. He married Harriet Eleanor "Nellie" McNair.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a life member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA and one of the founders and the associate president of the Gate City Free Kindergarten Association. They were the parents of Grace Towns Hamilton.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mortuary Owner. Trimble began his career in the funeral industry at age twelve sweeping the floors of Hanley's Bell Street Funeral Home. He opened his own mortuary in 1983. At the height of Trimble's career, his mortuary handled an average of eight hundred funerals per year. Trimble was known for his meticulous attention to detail in funeral arrangements and also for the lavish entertainments he held in his home. Trimble staged his final party at his house in Decatur, Georgia-he had left specific instructions regarding his wake. His body, clothed in a red silk embroidered dressing gown, was to be laid out for viewing in his bedroom, his eyeglasses and Bible arranged beside him on ivory satin sheets. Thousands came to view Trimble's body, and thousands more attended his funeral.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Legislator. Bishop Turner was a leader in the AME Church and a Georgia state legislator during Reconstruction. His fourth wife was noted religious worker Laura Pearl Lemon.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Married to Henry McNeal Turner.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Originally named "Basil" for the herb her mother loved to use as a seasoning, Usher changed her name to the more feminine "Bazoline" when she entered Atlanta University. Usher began her career at the American Missionary Association high school in Virginia. She returned to Atlanta to teach then began moving into administrative positions-elementary school principal at Wesley Avenue, vice principal at Booker T. Washington High, principal at Howard Junior High. She also completed a master's degree at Atlanta University. In 1951, she was appointed director of instruction for African American students in Atlanta schools-she was the only African American at the time to have an office in City Hall. She was responsible for opening seven new elementary schools during her tenure. In 1943, Usher organized the first African American Girl Scout troop in Atlanta. She was also an avid sports fan and tennis player, and for two years she was the city's African American female tennis champion. A public school was named in her honor, and in 2014 she was designated a Georgia Woman of Achievement.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician and Surgeon. Orphaned at the age of three, Wallace had no formal schooling until age thirteen. He started his education at Georgia State College in Savannah. He worked his way through Clark College in Atlanta, then Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee. After completing his medical degree, Wallace opened a practice in Atlanta, and a drugstore, the Junction Pharmacy. He also served as secretary of the Atlanta Medical Association. He married Birdie Florence Crolley.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was the daughter of John and Mary Crolley. She was a member of Warren Memorial United Methodist Church and president of the Women's Home Missionary Society, the Women's Society of Christian Service, and United Methodist Women. Active in community and civic affairs, she worked in the presidential campaign of Harry Truman in 1948, and she volunteered in the first Community Chest Drive and in membership drives for the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA. She was one of the organizers of the Sadie Mays nursing home. A graduate of Clark College, she worked as an insurance sales agent following her husband's death.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Son of Edward and Birdie Wallace, he was one of the first African Americans to join the Marines. In 2011, he and fellow African Americans who trained at Montford Point from 1942 to 1949 were awarded the Congressional Gold Medal "for outstanding perseverance and courage." After his 1974 retirement from a career in the U.S. Postal Service, Wallace served as Senate Doorkeeper in the Georgia Legislature for eighteen sessions. He was appointed Sergeant at Arms for the senate and held that position from 2007 until 2010. A lifetime member of Warren Memorial, he served as church historian. In 2004, he helped organize the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation and served as its first treasurer.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Watson was President of Arkansas Agricultural, Mechanical, and Normal College (now the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff). He earned a bachelor of philosophy degree in 1904 from Brown University. He was mentored by fellow Brown University graduate John Hope, the first African American president of Morehouse College. Watson served as professor of mathematics and science at Morehouse from 1904 to 1908. After leaving Morehouse, he served as secretary of the Colored Men's Department of the International Committee of the YMCA. Watson Memorial Library on the University of Arkansas campus at Pine Bluff was named in his memory. He married Hattie Louise Gertrude Rutherford.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She graduated from Spelman College and earned a master's degree in library science from Atlanta University. She taught at Morehouse and was one of the founders of Atlanta's Neighborhood Union. She served on the trustee boards of Atlanta University, Spelman, and Morehouse. At Arkansas A & M, she and her husband founded and co-edited the newspaper, The Arkansawyer. She opened and operated the first bookstore on campus, and she helped raise tuition for needy students. She worked in the Arkansas A & M library until 1971 and organized the first acquisition of books by and about African Americans.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner, Co-founder of South-View Cemetery. He was the father of South-View Secretary Lewis Gould Watts and grandfather of South-View President Albert Hawes Watts.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Son of South-View co-founder Albert Watts. He served as secretary of South-View Cemetery.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Grandson of South-View co-founder Albert Watts. He served as president of South-View Cemetery.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Concert Promoter. During the height of the Great Depression in 1937, Watts used her own funds to bring contralto Marian Anderson to Detroit, Michigan, for her first performance in that city. For twenty-five years, the Nellie Watts Concert Series was an annual tradition in Detroit. It featured artists such as Anderson, Leontyne Price, and Paul Robeson. Robeson, who insisted on being presented by her, dubbed Watts "a fine impresario." The Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre also performed in Watts' concert series. Watts founded the Patron of the Arts organization in Detroit to provide funding for the series and to encourage aspiring performers. Watts was a graduate of Atlanta University and Detroit Teacher's College. She was a teacher in the Detroit public schools, an active clubwoman, and a board member of the Detroit NAACP. She was the daughter of South-View founder Albert Watts.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Weatherspool was a graduate of Florida A & M College. He also attended Walker Baptist Institute in Augusta, Georgia, and Moody Bible Institute and the American Bible School, both in Chicago, Illinois. He was pastor of Mount Olive Baptist Church in Atlanta for forty-five years. Mount Olive was in debt $35,000 when he arrived as pastor; the church was worth a million dollars by the time of his retirement. Weatherspool Hall at Mount Olive was named in his honor. Weatherspool was a member of the Atlanta Political and Civic League, a leader in the Atlanta Negro Voters League, and co-chair of the Atlanta Bi-Partisan Voters League. Weatherspool died just five weeks after celebrating his 100th birthday. He married Lillie Sirmans.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. A graduate of Spelman College, she earned a master's degree at Atlanta University. She was a teacher in Alabama and Georgia high schools. She served as president of the Women's Convention of the General Missionary Baptist Convention of Georgia, and she served on the board of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA. She was also a member of the Atlanta Metropolitan Council of Negro Women.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: First Lieutenant Walter D. Westmoreland graduated from Morehouse College and received his master's degree from Atlanta University. He earned his pilot wings at the Moton Field flight facility in Tuskegee, Alabama. As a Tuskegee Airman, he was one of the African American pilots who served in combat with the Army air forces during WWII. Westmoreland flew with the 302nd Fighter Squadron of the 332nd Fighter Group, stationed in Italy. Each fighter group painted the tails of their aircraft to uniquely identify them. The members of the 332nd used solid red, hence their nickname, the "Red Tails." Westmoreland's plane was shot down while providing air support for the beach landing at the port of Anzio in Italy. When he bailed from the disabled aircraft, he broke his leg in two places. After recuperating in a field hospital, he chose to continue flying. His plane was again shot down on October 13, 1944, while returning from an escort mission to Blechammer, Germany. Westmoreland was killed; his body was ultimately recovered and returned to Atlanta in 1949. Westmoreland was the son of William G. Westmoreland.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Postal Worker. William Westmoreland graduated from Atlanta University. After retiring from the postal service, he worked in real estate and insurance. Westmoreland died just days before his son's body was due to arrive in Atlanta. A double funeral was held for father and son at First Congregational Church.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Carpenter, Cotton Classer, Fraternal Leader. Whitaker worked as a carpenter and later as a cotton classer for the George H. McFadden Agency in Atlanta. He was prominent in fraternal circles and served as the state grand secretary of the Good Samaritans for twenty-five years. He was also a Mason and an Odd Fellow. Whitaker traveled often on fraternal business for the Good Samaritans, which included trips to the Bahamas, Turks and Caicos, and Cuba. He married Dora B. Ector. Noted for his advocacy of cooperative business ventures for African Americans, he purchased stock in various organizations and served as a director in the Standard Loan and Realty Company, the Service Company, and the South-View Cemetery Association.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a secretary for the Good Samaritans and worked as a bookkeeper for an insurance company. She was a charter member of the Neighborhood Union. The Whitakers' grandson, William W. Allison, was the founding chairman of the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Rapper. Known as Bankroll Fresh, in 2014, White released his breakout mixtape called Life of a Hot Boy. He released Life of a Hot Boy 2: Real Trapper and his self-titled mixtape Bankroll Fresh in 2015. His single, "Take Over Your Trap," featured an appearance by 2 Chainz. He starred in a short film inspired by the single, also titled "Take Over Your Trap," produced by Worldwide Street Money. White also appeared on 2 Chainz's T.R.U. Jack City mixtape.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Author. Whiting was a graduate of Howard University, in Washington, D. C. and taught at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Considered a pioneer in progressive elementary education, she was appointed coordinator for the Jeanes teachers program in Georgia. Whiting also held various other positions in Georgia education-she was principal of the elementary department of the laboratory school at Atlanta University, State Supervisor of African American elementary schools, and coordinator of student teaching at the Georgia Department of Education. Whiting served on several national educational committees, including President Herbert Hoover's White House Conference on Child Health and Protection, the Committee on Elementary Education, and the National Conference on the Fundamental Problems in Negro Education. Whiting published two books for children that emphasized African American history and heritage: Negro Folk Tales for Children of Primary Grades and Negro Art, Music, Rhyme, and Dance for Young Folks. A school in Tucker, Georgia, was named in her honor. She married Joseph L. Whiting.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator. Whiting served as director of education at Tuskegee before being appointed as a YMCA secretary in Montoir, France, during WWI. He recruited teacher-soldiers to educate illiterate African American servicemen in anticipation of their return to civilian life in the U.S. In Atlanta, Whiting was a professor of education at Atlanta University.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Poet. Whitman was born enslaved in Kentucky. After the end of the Civil War, he worked in manual labor jobs. He was primarily self-taught, however, with only a few months of schooling he began to teach. He entered Wilberforce University but only stayed for six months. It was at Wilberforce that he met the school's president, Bishop Daniel Alexander Payne of the AME Church. Whitman became Bishop Payne's protege. He founded and pastored churches in Ohio, Kansas, Texas, and Georgia, and he served as the general financial agent at Wilberforce. In Atlanta, Whitman pastored Allen Temple. While following the ministry, Whitman also found time to write. He also composed one of the longest poems ever written by an African American, "Not a Man and Yet a Man." He was the first African American to publish a poem in Spenserian stanza, "Twasinta's Seminoles." Whitman struggled with alcoholism throughout his life, and his addiction may have hampered both his ministerial and writing career. He married Caddie (aka Katie) Whitman.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was a skilled orator and the president of the Women's Council of the Nineteenth Century. The organization, which Caddie Whitman founded, encouraged African American women's participation in the moral growth and future of the race. In 1893, on "Colored Americans' Day" at Chicago's World Columbian Exhibition, she read her husband's poem, "Freedom's Triumphant Song," a composition he wrote for the occasion. They were parents of "The Whitman Sisters," a traveling vaudeville act. Caddie Whitman was not only her daughters' chaperone on the road but also their first business manager-unusual in a time when white American men generally managed African American performers on the vaudeville circuit.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: The Whitman Sisters, Mabel, Essie, and Alberta, were part of a vaudeville touring act in the early part of the twentieth century. They were the daughters of Albery Alison and Caddie Whitman. The sisters began singing, dancing, and playing guitar in their father's church and later, Mabel and Essie, billed as "The Danzette Sisters," toured throughout the South and in Europe. Alberta joined the group and the sisters continued to tour on both the white and African American vaudeville circuits. The sisters were light skinned enough to pass for white and sometimes wore blackface makeup while performing. In 1904, they made news by demanding that the Jefferson theater in Birmingham, Alabama, integrate seating on the main floor. Mabel was the eldest sister and followed her mother as the group's manager. Essie had a distinct contralto voice and was a quick-witted comedian. She designed and made the group's costumes. Essie became a preacher in Chicago after her retirement from show business, and the sisters bought a home together in the city. Alberta, called Bert, was a flash dancer and a celebrated male impersonator. She handled the music and composed much of the group's material. Performing as the "Whitman Sisters Revue," the company grew to more than forty performers, including Eddie "Rochester" Anderson, Count Basie, and Moms Mabley. Twelve-year-old tap dancer Bill "Bojangles" Robinson got his start with the Whitman sisters. After Caddie Whitman's death in 1909, a much younger, fourth "sister," Alice, joined the group. Alice was a tap dancer and champion cakewalk dancer. Alice is buried in Chicago, Illinois. Their older brother, Caswell Woodfin Whitman, also a talented musician, is buried in the family plot at South-View.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Older brother of the Whitman Sisters and son of Albery Alison and Caddie Whitman, he was also a talented musician and is buried in the family plot at South-View.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister. Wilkes was elected the sixty-ninth bishop of the AME Church in 1948. He served the church as bishop for twenty-eight years and presided over five Episcopal districts during his tenure. Under the leadership of Bishop Wilkes, in 1958, the Turner Theological Seminary became part of the Interdenominational Theological Center. He was chair of the board of trustees at his alma mater, Morris Brown College. Wilkes served as president of the Atlanta Chapter of the NAACP. His epitaph reads "I have given them thy word."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Civil Rights Leader. In his first year as Ebenezer's pastor, Williams grew the congregation from just a handful to more than sixty members. He developed Ebenezer as a religious institution that also served as a center for political and community activities. In 1917, he helped organize the Atlanta branch of the NAACP and later served as its president. Williams was president of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers' Union, and he received the doctor of divinity degree from Morehouse College. He married Jennie Celeste Parks.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She was involved in most aspects of church governance at Ebenezer and led the church's missionary society for many years. She represented the church in local Baptist organizations and in the Women's Convention, an auxiliary to the National Baptist Convention. The couple's daughter, Alberta Williams King, was the mother of Martin Luther King Jr.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Domestic Servant. Williams, born during slavery, was the namesake for a popular Smyrna, Georgia, restaurant called "Aunt Fanny's Cabin." The restaurant was owned by a member of the white American Campbell family that Williams had worked for during slavery and in freedom. Images of Williams, dressed in a white head kerchief and apron, were featured in the restaurant's advertising. Williams was active in her community and at the Wheat Street Baptist Church. She received an award for being the top fundraiser in a campaign to build a hospital for African Americans in Marietta.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Educator, Civil Rights Leader. A native of Arkansas, Williams earned undergraduate degrees at Morehouse College and Howard University. He continued his studies at Howard to earn a master's degree, and he completed doctoral degrees at the University of Chicago and Arkansas Baptist College. In Atlanta, Williams was pastor of Friendship Baptist Church from 1954 until his death. He also served as chairman and professor in the philosophy and religion department at Morehouse College. Active in civic affairs, Williams was president of the Atlanta Branch of the NAACP and a member of the executive committee. In 1959, he was one of the plaintiffs in a successful Atlanta city bus desegregation lawsuit. He held various leadership positions in the SCLC, the Atlanta Summit Leadership Conference, the Greater Atlanta Council on Human Relations, and the Georgia Council on Human Relations. His widow, Billye Williams, married major league baseball player Hank Aaron.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Realtist, City Councilman, Civil Rights Leader. Williamson was the first African American elected to Atlanta's City Council since Reconstruction.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Singer, Songwriter. Born in Atlanta, Willis gained his early performance experience with local band leaders like Red McAllister Riggins. Willis' style was grounded in gospel-based blues ballads, but in his later years he became a popular rock-and-roll artist. Willis is best remembered for his hit "C. C. Rider," an old blues standard originally recorded by Ma Rainey. Nicknamed "Sheik of the Shake" and the "King of the Stroll," he often performed wearing one of his signature turbans. Two of Willis' songs hit the charts after his death: "What Am I Living For" and "Hang Up My Rock and Roll Shoes." Willis died at the age of thirty after undergoing surgery at an Atlanta hospital for an infected stomach ulcer.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Minister, Reporter. Wingfield was a presiding elder and official reporter for the AME Church. In addition to his regular contributions to the Southern Christian Recorder and the Western Recorder, he also wrote articles for the Atlanta Daily World, the Atlanta Journal, and the Atlanta Constitution. Wingfield was a mission builder and was responsible for the organization of a number of churches, including the John Alexander Memorial AME Church. An early influence in his life was Bishop Henry McNeal Turner, with whom he lived as a child. He married Bessie L. Williams.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Born in Warrington, Georgia, she attended Spelman College in Atlanta. After graduation, she returned home and worked for a time as a clerk in her father's business. She held various positions in the Women's Home and Foreign Mission Society.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Educator, Journalist. Woolcock was a teacher in the Atlanta Public Schools, and she served as the women's page editor for the Atlanta Daily World. She wrote the popular "Social Swirl" column from 1943 to 1989. Woolcock also covered the Metropolitan Opera's annual May performance in Atlanta. She enjoyed attending the opera, the symphony, and the theater. She was a world traveler and wrote a travelogue of her experiences. Woolcock was a member of the Atlanta Association of Media Women. She married Harold H. Barrington Woolcock.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Blues Singer. In 1940s Atlanta, Wright was called the "Prince of the Blues." He had a high-pitched vocal range, wore his hair styled in a pompadour, and dressed elaborately for the stage. All of which "Little Richard" Penniman acknowledged he copied from Wright, the man he called his idol. Wright was born in Atlanta and began singing gospel music as a child at Mount Vernon Baptist Church. Wright was not only a popular entertainer in Atlanta, he also performed at venues such as the Apollo Theater in New York City and the Howard Theater in Washington, D. C. Wright began recording with Savoy records in 1949 and released a number of top ten records, including "Blues for My Baby," "Stacked Deck," and "Hey Little Girl."
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Community Volunteer. Wynn was a co-founder of the Gate City Free Kindergarten Association, established in 1905. She chaired the association's board of directors. The Ida E. Wynn Day Care Center was named in her honor. An Atlanta native, Wynn attended Atlanta University. She was a life member of the Phyllis Wheatley YWCA. She married William Andrew Wynn.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Born in Hancock County, Georgia, Wynn came to Atlanta to attend Morehouse College. He worked as a mail carrier. Wynn was one of the founders of the Atlanta YMCA for African Americans. He also served on the YMCA board and in the role of treasurer.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Physician. Yancey was the first African American member of the faculty of Emory University's medical school, and he was also the first African American doctor at Grady Memorial Hospital. Yancey graduated from Morehouse College and the University of Michigan Medical School. He studied under Dr. Charles R. Drew at Freedmen's Hospital at the Howard University School of Medicine in Washington, D.C. He served as chief of surgery at Tuskegee Veterans Hospital for ten years before joining the faculty at Emory. In 1972, he became the medical director at Grady Hospital. Yancey also served as a member of the Atlanta school board. He was the son of mail carrier Arthur Henry Yancey and Daisy Lois Sherard. He married Carolyn E. "Marge" Yancey.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Father of Dr. Asa Greenwood Yancey. Arthur Yancey was a mail carrier and served as president of the Atlanta Letter Carriers Association, a professional organization for African American postal workers. Arthur Yancey was also a frequent contributor to the Atlanta Daily World through his letters to the editor. In 1920, Arthur Yancey, his wife, and their infant son Orlando traveled to Brazil where Yancey planned to start an export business. While in Brazil, he was attracted to Catholicism and the work the church was doing among the Brazilian people. When he returned to Atlanta, he converted to Catholicism and began his work in the Catholic Church. In 1960, at his parish, St. Paul of the Cross, Yancey was recognized by the Pope for his faith and devotion and was given the medal Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice, one of the highest awards of the Vatican. After his retirement, in 1959, he wrote an autobiographical account of his life in rural Georgia told in sketches, stories, and poems.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Mother of Dr. Asa Greenwood Yancey. Daisy Yancey attended Atlanta public schools and the Atlanta University Normal School. She was elected president of the Neighborhood Union in 1950 and served until the organization officially disbanded in 1962.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: She graduated from Wayne University in Detroit, Michigan, and taught in Detroit elementary schools. In Atlanta, she served on the board of trustees at Spelman College. She was the first African American female to be appointed to the Georgia Board of Regents. She was a member of the Atlanta Board of Education, and she was affiliated with the League of Women Voters, the Atlanta Urban League, and the NAACP.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Business Owner. Yates, a graduate of Morehouse College, was co-owner and chief operating officer of the Yates and Milton Drugstore chain. He served as board chair of Citizens Trust Bank. He also served as president of the South-View Cemetery Association. He was the first African American named to the Fulton-DeKalb County Hospital Authority. Yates served as vice president of both the Southeastern Fire Insurance Company and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan. He married Mae Maxwell.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Social Worker. She succeeded her mother, Clara M. Pitts, as director of the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home (CSPH). At the time of Yates' appointment in 1950, CSPH was still the only full-time child care agency in Atlanta for African American children. Under her direction, the home continued to expand and modernize its facilities, and in 1964 she relocated CSPH to Fairburn Road. The new location featured cottage-style residences for the children plus room for future expansion. She served on the faculty of Atlanta University's School of Social Work and was a charter member of the National Association of Social Workers. She was the first recipient of the Atlanta Urban League's Jesse O. Thomas Community Service Award.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Librarian. Yates was the first African American director of the Atlanta-Fulton Public Library system (AFPL). A Spelman College graduate, she earned a master's degree in library science from Atlanta University in 1951. She worked in libraries in New Jersey and New York before being appointed AFPL director in 1976. She also earned a law degree from the Atlanta Law School. She served on the governing Council and Executive Board of the American Library Association (ALA), and she helped originate the ALA's Coretta Scott King Book Award.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

people.biography: Butler. Young worked as a waiter at several Atlanta restaurants before joining the staff of the Georgia governor's mansion during the administration of Carl Sanders, from 1963 to 1967. At that time, the governor's mansion was located in Atlanta's Ansley Park. In 1967, a new gubernatorial residence was completed on West Paces Ferry Road, and Young continued to work on the mansion staff when Lester Maddox took office on January 1, 1968. During his tenure at the governor's mansion, Young served four additional Georgia governors: Jimmy Carter, George Busbee, Joe Frank Harris, and Zell Miller.
people.source: Henderson, D.L. South-View: City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.

faqs.q: When was South-View Cemetery founded?
faqs.a: South-View Cemetery was chartered on April 26, 1886, by six formerly enslaved African American men in Atlanta, Georgia.

faqs.q: Who founded South-View Cemetery?
faqs.a: South-View was founded by Albert Watts, Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Robert Grant, Charles H. Morgan, and John Render — all formerly enslaved African Americans.

faqs.q: Why was South-View Cemetery created?
faqs.a: South-View was created because of the indignities African Americans faced at Atlanta's segregated cemeteries — particularly Oakland Cemetery's 'Slave Square' (whose occupants were mass-exhumed in 1877) and Westview's segregated 'Rest Haven.' Albert Watts was moved to action after watching his father buried through Westview's back gate in October 1885.

faqs.q: Is Martin Luther King Jr. buried at South-View Cemetery?
faqs.a: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was temporarily buried at South-View in 1968 after his assassination, but his remains were later moved to the MLK Center for Nonviolent Social Change in Atlanta. However, his parents — Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King — ARE permanently interred at South-View in a marble crypt.

faqs.q: How many people are buried at South-View?
faqs.a: More than 70,000 people are buried at South-View, with hundreds of new burials each year.

faqs.q: Where is South-View Cemetery located?
faqs.a: South-View Cemetery is at 1990 Jonesboro Road SE, Atlanta, Georgia 30315, in the Lakewood Heights neighborhood — about 15 minutes from downtown Atlanta.

faqs.q: What are South-View Cemetery's hours?
faqs.a: South-View is open Monday through Sunday, 9:00am to 5:00pm. Phone: (404) 622-5393.

faqs.q: Is South-View an active cemetery?
faqs.a: Yes. South-View is an active cemetery with thousands of burial spaces available and undeveloped land to keep it operational for decades.

faqs.q: What is South-View's historical significance?
faqs.a: South-View is the oldest African American cemetery in Atlanta and the oldest African American non-eleemosynary (non-charitable) stockholder corporation in the United States. It has served as the final resting place for over 70,000 African Americans from Reconstruction to the present, documenting the full sweep of Black Atlanta history.

faqs.q: Who is Alonzo Herndon?
faqs.a: Alonzo Franklin Herndon was born into slavery but became Atlanta's first Black millionaire. He established a chain of successful barbershops and founded the Atlanta Life Insurance Company. He is buried at South-View Cemetery.

faqs.q: Can I take a tour of South-View Cemetery?
faqs.a: Yes. South-View offers docent-led walking tours of notable gravesites, group tours by reservation, and a free self-guided cell phone walking/driving tour.

faqs.q: Who was Georgia's first Black registered nurse?
faqs.a: Ludie Clay Andrews (d. 1969) was the first African American registered nurse in Georgia. She organized the Grady Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses in 1914. She is buried at South-View.

faqs.q: Who was Georgia's first Black licensed pharmacist?
faqs.a: Moses Amos (d. 1928) passed the Georgia state pharmacy exam in June 1911 and became the first African American granted a druggist license by the Georgia State Board of Pharmacy. He is buried at South-View.

faqs.q: What was WERD radio station?
faqs.a: WERD was the first radio station in the United States owned by African Americans. Jesse Bee Blayton (d. 1977) — Georgia's first Black CPA and a Mutual Federal Savings founder — purchased WERD in 1949. Blayton is buried at South-View.

faqs.q: Who was Grace Towns Hamilton?
faqs.a: Grace Towns Hamilton (d. 1992) was the first African American woman elected as a state legislator in the Deep South. She served in the Georgia legislature from 1965 to 1984 and was a principal architect of the 1973 Atlanta city charter. She is buried at South-View.

faqs.q: Is South-View Cemetery on the National Register of Historic Places?
faqs.a: South-View was listed on the Georgia Register of Historic Places in 2026 and a National Register of Historic Places nomination was submitted (NPS reference BC100013186). The nomination was coordinated with the Atlanta Preservation Center.

faqs.q: Which Atlanta Child Murder victims are buried at South-View?
faqs.a: Seven victims of the 1979-1981 Atlanta Child Murders are buried at South-View: Milton Harvey, Yusef Bell, Aaron Wyche, Aaron Jackson, Patrick Rogers, Curtis Walker, and William Barrett.

faqs.q: What athletes are buried at South-View?
faqs.a: Notable athletes include Walter Jones Bellamy (1960 Olympic gold medalist, 1962 NBA Rookie of the Year, Basketball Hall of Fame 1993), David T. Harper (Negro League outfielder), and Hank Aaron (baseball legend).

faqs.q: Who manages South-View Cemetery?
faqs.a: South-View is managed by the South-View Cemetery Association. The Watts family has managed it from its earliest days. As of 2018, president Winifred Watts Hemphill is the great-granddaughter of founder Albert Watts.

faqs.q: What is the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation?
faqs.a: The Historic South-View Preservation Foundation is a nonprofit founded in 2004. It records, interprets, restores, and preserves the art, history, and environment of South-View's non-perpetual care sections. Historian D.L. Henderson joined its board in 2005 and wrote the 2018 book 'South-View: City of the Dead.'

faqs.q: Who is John Wesley Dobbs?
faqs.a: John Wesley Dobbs was a well-known Atlanta civic and political leader known as the 'Mayor of Sweet Auburn.' He is buried at South-View. His daughter Mattiwilda Dobbs was the first African American to sing a major role at Italy's La Scala opera house.

faqs.q: What book is this database based on?
faqs.a: This database is sourced from 'South-View: City of the Dead' by D.L. Henderson, published by Carrelspin Press, Dunwoody, Georgia, in 2018. ISBN 978-0-9985772-0-3. Henderson served as South-View's historian and developed its first public walking tour.

faqs.q: Who is Bishop Henry McNeal Turner?
faqs.a: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner (d. 1915) was a prominent African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church leader and a Reconstruction-era Georgia state legislator. He is buried at South-View.

faqs.q: What is the Founders Mausoleum at South-View?
faqs.a: The Founders Mausoleum opened at South-View Cemetery on August 1, 2009. It offers families an above-ground burial option.

faqs.q: What were Slave Square and Rest Haven?
faqs.a: Slave Square was the segregated African American burial section at Oakland Cemetery (est. 1850), with 860+ burials by the Civil War's end. In 1877, the Atlanta City Council voted to exhume and mass-reinter its occupants to resell the land. Rest Haven was the segregated African American section at Westview Cemetery (est. 1884), accessible only through a back gate. Both were direct causes of South-View's founding.
